14516:
I added Pinball I by Mark Keller.  This program was archived from an unpublished "Arcadian" submission tape (from 1980) in the Bob Fabris Collection.  This is a 2000-Bally "AstroBASIC" conversion of an original 300-baud BALLY BASIC program.

Pinball I is a simple pinball game (no gravity). It will prompt for parameters, triggers 1 & 2 control the flippers. [Use the player 1 trigger for the left flipper, and the player 2 trigger for the right flipper.] They stay on a set period of time when used and then are disabled for a set period of time.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#PinballIAstroBASIC

Here is a May 10, 2016 email that I sent to Paul Thacker about my conversion of the original Bally BASIC game:

"I loaded and tried "Pinball I" by Mark Keller.  This was only archived as a 300-baud program, so I loaded it via the Bally BASIC tape interface.  It loaded fine and played okay.  It's really quite slow.  I converted it to AstroBASIC using the 300-to-2000 baud converter program in the AstroBASIC manual.  I saved it to 2000 baud without making any changes at all.  I might need to insert NT=-1-- I'm not sure (I haven't looked at the code).  I played "Pinball I" under AstroBASIC and it plays SO much faster-- it's like a different game.  I'm really impressed.

"I've attached the 2000-baud file.  Could you look at it and load it to test it on your machine to make sure it works too?

"It turns out that I no longer seem to have any computers that can load/save 2000-baud programs with ease.  This old laptop can load AstroBASIC programs to the cartridge, but it just BARELY gets a signal from the AstroBASIC cart when :PRINT is used to save a program.  Luckily, I was able to use "amplify" in Audoacity, which allowed ballybin to work (where it failed on the unamplified file)."

Adam


Paul responded:

"Your recording worked for me. I didn't really have as good an experience with it, though. My ball got in a loop between a bumper and the top wall, which went on for 30 cycles or so. I was about ready to reset the game when it finally broke out. Of course, if it had been a high score competition, that would have helped me out.

"Just be sure to note when a game is a 300-to-2000 baud conversion. I believe this game was never published, so you may have been the first person ever to play it in 2000 baud format."

Paul

----------------------------------------

In an unpublished letter to Bob Fabris (dated November 1, 1981), Mark Keller wrote:

Dear Bob,

Here are the answers to your problems with my programs (I hope).  Lines 30-70 of Blockout 5.0 are:

50 CX=60;PRINT #2,L,
70 BOX C,-43,K,2,3;BOX Y,X,2,2,3

Yes, the line sequence in Pinball I goes 9, 10, 20, 40.

Both games ["Blockout" and "Pinball I"] were written as short, simple (and unfortunately slow) graphics games.

Blockout 5.0 is played like Breakout or Brickyard.  The game will prompt for parameters and hand controller #1 moves the paddle.

"Pinball I" is a simple pinball game (no gravity).  It will prompt for parameters, triggers 1 & 2 control the flippers.  They stay on a set period of time when used and then are disabled for a set period of time.  I'll send more game soon (I hope), and am now working on a Bally -> Vic-20 interface.

Mark


----------------------------------------


Enjoy this non-Pinball Pong-like Pinball game!

I added six alternate versions of the the Blue Ram Utility to BallyAlley.com:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/perkins_engineering.html#BlueRAMUtility

1) Blue Ram Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud) - archived from tape of many RAM expansion programs compiled by Mike White. Queue up both loads, enter ":INPUT; RUN" into AstroBASIC, and play.

2) Blue Ram Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud)[a] - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection. The tape has the official Perkins Engineering Blue Ram label, but the only identification of the program is a hand-written "Utility". Queue up both loads, enter ":INPUT; RUN" into AstroBASIC, and play. The code differs slightly from Blue Ram Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud). The tape has AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of the Blue Ram Utility on one side, and AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of Blue Ram Diagnostic on the other.

3) Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud) - archived from tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled "Blue Ram Utility 1.0 Copy". Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. The code matches a printout found in Bob Fabris's documents.

4) Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)[a] - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection . The tape has the official Perkins Engineering Blue Ram label, but the only identification of the program is a hand-written "Utility". Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. The BASIC code is identical to Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud), while the machine code portion differs slightly. Both versions seemed to process correctly, and to run alright. The tape has AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of the Blue Ram Utility on one side, and AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of Blue Ram Diagnostic on the other.

5) Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto) - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "BR UTIL". Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. As compared to the version I believe was the released one, it is missing the machine language portion. The BASIC code has several differences as compared to the other archived versions.

6) Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto)[a] - found in Bob Fabris's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "Blue Ram Utility". Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. As compared to the version I believe was the released one, it is missing the machine language portion. The BASIC code has several differences as compared to the other archived versions.

Including these six alternate versions of the Blue Ram Utility now takes the number of versions up to 13 alternates... which seems a bit excessive.  Still, if Paul's willing to put in the time to archive this stuff, then I'm willing to upload it.

14523:
I added two alternate versions the Blue Ram Utility by Perkins Engineering.  One of these is the first (and only) version of this program archived in 2000-baud format.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/perkins_engineering.html#BlueRAMDiagnostic

1) Blue Ram Diagnostic (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto) - archived from tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled simply "Blue Ram Diagnostic".  Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. It differs from the previously archived Blue Ram Diagnostic dated 6-2-80. I found that version in both Bob Fabris's and Ken Lill's collections. On one tape, it was labeled as version 1.0. This version has no date and no machine language portion, so I believe it is likely an earlier prototype.

2) Blue Ram Diagnostic (198x)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud) - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection.  The tape has the official Perkins Engineering Blue Ram label, but the only identification of the program is a hand-written "Diagnostic". The tape has AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of the Blue Ram Utility on one side, and AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of Blue Ram Diagnostic on the other. The tape label gives these loading instructions:

Astro INPUT; RUN Mode = RAM (Center)

There are two loads, the second one very short. I found this a little confusing, as the program started once the first load was finished, even if I only loaded it with :INPUT, not using RUN. The first line of the program does have a conditional :INPUT %(28672), so perhaps the second load would be used in specific circumstances. The test is IF A=0.


Thanks again to Paul for archiving these programs, and (just as importantly) for keeping great reference notes of the sources of these programs.

14524:
I added 1980's Music Compiler with Sarabande by Perkins Engineering for BALLY BASIC.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/Music%20Compiler%20and%20Sarabande%20(Perkins%20Engineering).zip

Paul wrote extensive notes when he archived this program with its music:

Music Compiler (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto) - found in Ken Lill's collection on a tape hand-labeled "Music Compiler". The other side contained Sarabande. I believe this should be loaded into Bally BASIC with :INPUT, followed by loading music data with :INPUT.

The first mention of this program is in Arcadian volume 2, issue 10, page 97, in which Perkins Engineering describes upcoming software for use with the Blue Ram expansion:

"Then we will provide the software necessary to have the Blue Ram act as a compiler for music programs. Using Processor Technology format, one can simply enter musical selections and the software will convert that into the proper language that the Bally can understand."

The next mention comes in Arcadian volume 3, issue 2, page 18. The news here talks about John Perkins giving a demonstration of the Blue Ram to a computer club:

"Next, we listened with pleasure to several Bally compiled musical selections from Bach and Handel in three part harmony. It was explained that the compiler is used to translate a person's own composition or regular sheet music into a form that is played by the Bally."

And that's actually the last I can find. The fact that it's never actually advertised makes me think that it was never released, although it clearly got to a point where it was usable.

The only music I found for this is Sarabande. Handel composed a song named Sarabande, so this fits with the newsletter. Unfortunately, the versions of Sarabande and Music Compiler seem to be incompatible. For example, they even use a different address range for storing the music data. I got some suggestions from Richard Degler, but even after cleaning up the Sarabande code and changing the address range, I still couldn't get Music Compiler to play music. If anyone figures out how to get this working, let us know.


Sarabande (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(Music Compiler)(proto) - for general information, see the Music Compiler description. This was found in Ken Lill's collection on a tape hand-labeled "Music - Sarabande". The other side contained Music Compiler. I believe this should be loaded into Bally BASIC with :INPUT after loading Music Compiler. Sarabande is a little strange because there are actually two sections on the tape, the second one much shorter and lower volume. The first section ends with U&(64)=0. The second has a few bytes not seen in the first section, then U&(64)=0 again, then a STOP TAPE message followed by :RETURN; RUN. My best guess was that the extra bytes and U&(64)=0 in the second part should be removed, but even doing this, and changing the address range to that used in Music Compiler, I still didn't manage to play a song. Therefore, I am uploading this exactly as I found it on the tape. If anyone figures out how to get this working, let us know.


That's the last of the programs for expanded BASIC that Paul has archived.  I'll begin to upload some Bally BASIC programs tomorrow.

14533:
Paul Thacker identified the unknown program "ZZZ-Unk Dice (19xx)(possibly Karl Nystrom)(300 baud)" as "Can You Quit" by Ken Lill.  The program has now been renamed and is in a new archive on BallyAlley.com (the old program name and archive has been deleted).  Also, several early prototype versions of this dice game have now been archived in the "Can You Quit" archive.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#CanYouQuiteBallyBASIC

The renamed version of the program is:

Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud) -  This program was found in Ken Lill's tape collection, on an unlabeled side of a tape.  Checkers, by Karl Nystrom, was on the other side of the tape.  On the same side, there was also a short
2000 baud unidentified program where you move around a submarine sprite (this program has been dubbed "Submarine").  Note, "Can You Quit" was originally archived as "ZZZ-Unk Dice (19xx)(possibly Karl Nystrom)(300 baud)."  However, it has now been properly identified and renamed to reflect the proper name.

Archive notes concerning the alternate versions of this program:

All of these were found on a tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled "At 0 @357=Logo, At 100 @257=STREAP, At 160 @258=Can You Quit". I'm not sure if I read the number 357 correctly.

The following four programs were on a single side of the tape.

1) Logo (for Starship and Can You Quit) (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto) - A logo screen that says this is Tape #1 from Gambits, and that Side 1 contains "Starship!" and Side 2 contains "Can You Quit?".

2) Starship (19xx)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a2] - A version of Starship that controls a little differently than the previously archived versions. Push the joystick left and pull the trigger to use guns, and push it right and pull the trigger to use bombs. It also seems unfinished. Once your ammo is depleted, there seems to be nothing to do other than wait to be destroyed. [Note: This "AstroBASIC" program is archived in the "Starship" archive.]

3) Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto) - A version of "Can You Quit?" that draws a diamond-shaped board, rolls some dice, and then appears to freeze up. I'd actually seen a version of this before, but hadn't been able to identify it. I had named it "ZZZ-UNK-Dice (19xx)(possibly Karl Nystrom)(300 baud)", but will now suggest it be named "Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)". I never figured out the rules to the game, but the previously archived one at least seems playable.

4) Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto)[a] - Another version of "Can You Quit?". It looks very similar to the previous load, but now there's a line moving over some of the dice. I still couldn't find a way to interact with it, though.

So far as Paul is aware, none of these programs were ever released for sale.

Thanks to Paul for figuring out another Bally mystery... and writing documentation and notes that allowed me to update the website easily.

1) Logo (for Starship and Can You Quit) (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto) - A logo screen that says this is Tape #1 from Gambits, and that Side 1 contains "Starship!" and Side 2 contains "Can You Quit?".

2) Starship (19xx)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a2] - A version of Starship that controls a little differently than the previously archived versions. Push the joystick left and pull the trigger to use guns, and push it right and pull the trigger to use bombs. It also seems unfinished. Once your ammo is depleted, there seems to be nothing to do other than wait to be destroyed. [Note: This "AstroBASIC" program is archived in the "Starship" archive.]

3) Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto) - A version of "Can You Quit?" that draws a diamond-shaped board, rolls some dice, and then appears to freeze up. I'd actually seen a version of this before, but hadn't been able to identify it. I had named it "ZZZ-UNK-Dice (19xx)(possibly Karl Nystrom)(300 baud)", but will now suggest it be named "Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)". I never figured out the rules to the game, but the previously archived one at least seems playable.

4) Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto)[a] - Another version of "Can You Quit?". It looks very similar to the previous load, but now there's a line moving over some of the dice. I still couldn't find a way to interact with it, though.

So far as Paul is aware, none of these programs were ever released for sale.

Thanks to Paul for figuring out another Bally mystery... and writing documentation and notes that allowed me to update the website easily.

Adam

14543:
I have added correspondence from 1985 and 1986 between Michael Matte, Don Gladden (who edited volume 6 of the Arcadian) and Bob Fabris.  Michael wrote the documentation on how to upgrade the Bally Arcade to hi-res mode.  His letter primarily deal with this matter, but he also drops some wonderful tid-bits, such as that he made a BalCheck II for his hi-res unit.  He also upgrade the Machine Language Manager cartridge so that it could take advantage of hi-res mode.


Michael's Astrocade High-Resolution Upgrade documentation is available here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html


I have added the correspondence to this upgrade area.  I've also revamped the entire area.  I added details about what is in the documentation "packages" that Michael wrote (I'll explain that in more detail in another post that I'll make soon).


Some of the letters were typed and some were handwritten by the authors.  I have used a combination of retyping, OCR and voice-to-text (using Dragon) to make the letters into text files (and searchable pdfs, in the case of the typed letters).  Rather than linking to the letters, I'm going going to include them in-full here:


1) Letter to Don Gladden from Michael Matte (June 7 and 8, 1985)


June 7, 1985


Dear Don:

I personally would like to have the option of programming on a high resolution screen. I have interfaced Texas Instrument's TMS9918A video display processor with my Astrocade computer, the chip having a high resolution mode, but I would prefer to program on a high resolution screen mapped by Bally's custom address and data chips because Bally's high resolution map (320 x 204 pixels) is easier to work with. Recently I have attempted to get my Astrocade computer to operate in the high resolution mode. I was aware that Datamax Inc. manufactured the Datamax UV-1 computer (16K ROM, 16K Screen RAM, and 32K User RAM) which utilized Bally's 3 custom address, data and I/O chips. In July of 1984, per my request, Datamax sent me copies, for a price, of electronic schematics and PC board layouts, but to my surprise, the copies were for their upgraded UV-1R (32K ROM, 256 Multipage Screen RAM, and 32K User RAM) computer.

With the aid of these schematics I came up with a scheme allowing my Astrocade computer to operate in the low or high resolution mode. Unfortunately, there's a "bug" in my scheme. I can display the high resolution map, write to it or read from it, and perform all the magic functions on it, but I get these glitches on the screen, occasionally, which appear and disappear. I used 0.1uf bypass capacitors judiciously for the four 16k banks of Screen RAM (I used type MK4116N-4 chips) and all other chips. I think the problem is somewhere in the timing.

Datamax's CPU board layout, where the Bally custom address and data chips are located, doesn't quite agree with its CPU board schematic, i.e., some resistors and capacitors appear on the CPU board layout but NOT on the CPU schematic. Datamax's scheme for the microcycler is almost identical to Bally/Astrocade's microcycler. Datamax added a chip to their microcycler which doesn't look like it's wired correctly (a drafting error?) and I haven't been able to figure out the reason for that additional chip due to lack of appropriate information on the Bally custom address and data chips. True, the Dave Nutting Associates manual provides information on the 3 custom chips, but offers no help as to how one would wire the required four 4K banks of screen RAM (and microcycler?) to get the high resolution map. What I would like to do is get my hands on copies of Datamax's UV-1 computer back in 1981 when it was a simpler system having only 16K ROM, 16K Screen RAM, and 32K User RAM.

I said all of this hoping the Arcadian might be able to help me out. How many other Bally/Astrocade computer users would be interested in expanding their system to provide an optional Bally high resolution map? Could you possibly print the following ad in the Arcadian? [I couldn't find the ad that Michael refers to to in the Fabris Collection, unless Michael is referring to the entire second part of his letter, dated the next day.]

--------------------

June 8, 1985

Dear Don:

I would like to provide for each new issue of the Arcadian an article on machine language programming for the Bally/ Astrocade computer. Hopefully the article would generate interest in some users to explore this powerful language. Perhaps programs with complex graphics might be created as a result of this interest.

With regard to submitting my articles to you, I have no idea as to how the Arcadian produces some of its articles with such small print. The only printer I have is an electrical typewriter. I could submit my articles to you using a double column on a 7" x 9.5" space giving you room for a border line, the Arcadian logo and so on. Would I be allowed to fill 3 pages (sides)? I have a lot of information to share, information that I haven't seen in the Arcadian (Vol. 4-6). Please give me some input regarding article submittals.

I realize you don't know what my background in machine language programming is. My articles will stress examples. Let my examples establish my credibility. I can show how to create fast non-blinking graphics.

This paragraph is for the Arcadian's information (for whatever its worth) that we users might pool our resources and continue support of the Bally/Astrocade computer. I haven't submitted any written material to the Arcadian previously because I have been working on projects for use with my Astrocade computer, projects such as:

1. A substitution for the Bally/Astrocade AC power transformer

2. Adding (or replacing RF modulator with) a composite video output and audio output for improved picture and sound

3. Interfacing Texas Instrument's TMS9918A video display processor

4. Adding 32K dynamic RAM addressed 8000-FFFFH and

5. Adding switchable 12K static RAM addressed 5000-7FFFH along with a video-cade copier connector.

I plan to build an eprom programmer that can be used with the Bally/Astrocade computer so that 2K, 4K and 8K EPROMS can be "burned", I also plan to develop a troubleshooting procedure and troubleshooting/check program for a Bally/Astrocade motherboard and hopefully any memory add-on. Incidentally, substitutions or equivalent replacements for any electrical/electronic component in the Bally/Astrocade computer will continue to be easily available, with the exception of the 3 custom chips and perhaps the +10V voltage regulator LM342P-10 (component #VR2). Most probably, the 3 custom chips will eventually be unavailable. The +10V voltage regulator is not used often and may eventually be unavailable. Jameco Electronics (415-592-8097), for example, is clearing out their stock of the IM342P-10 (it is listed in their flyer #127). For those who have committed themselves to the use of their Bally/Astrocade computer (I know I have), my advice is to take advantage of ABC Hobbycraft's sale on Astrocade units for $34.95 and motherboards for $5.00 so you have some back up parts while they are still cheap and available.

Sincerely,
Michael C. Matte


2) Letter to Bob Fabris By Michael Matte (December 21, 1985)

Dear Robert:

Thanks for responding to my 8 June and 7 June letters sent to Don Gladden, whom I have not received a response from.

I have a lot of information that I would like to share with the ARCADIAN. However, I question some of the information that I have as to whether or not you can publish it due to possible infringements on copyrights or perhaps patents. What I will do is send my own creations (tutorials, upgrades, whatever) to Don Gladden and to you I will send any questionable material indicating the source(s) of info for you to do with as you desire. It is my desire that support of the Astrocade home computer will continue.

Right now I have doubts that the ARCADIAN will continue publishing issues. Upon receipt of the next issue (Dec. ’85?), I will send an article to Don detailing a power transformer substitution for the Astrocade computer. After receipt of each future issue of the ARCADIAN, I will send to Don a tutorial on programming the Astrocade computer in machine language. I have already written several tutorials on this subject just waiting to be submitted to the ARCADIAN. Further material on other subjects will be sent to Don or yourself, of course at my discretion.

You asked me if I was aware of the Balchek program. Did you know that there exists a Balchek II? Yes, there is! Balchek II is an improved version of Balchek enabling its user to also check a RAM add-on. I have gone through the disassembled listing of Balcheck, have made some changes and deleted some of the useless routines to allow room to check a RAM add-on. Yes, Balchek II does exist, although not quite finished yet. I have a copy of it on tape. Wish you could see it.

There is something else I wish you could see. That is, the Astrocade home computer running with a high resolution map (320x204 pixels). What a difference! I have resolved the high resolution glitch problem described in my June '85 letter I sent to Don. I am currently writing an 8K byte software package to be eventually burned on an EPROM. The package will contain an improved 2K byte high resolution version of Bit Fiddler’s MLM, 2K bytes for 33 high resolution subroutines (similar to the onboard subroutines) and 4K bytes devoted to extended high resolution graphic subroutines. My Astrocade computer can now operate with a low or high resolution map. Unfortunately, modifications were required on the motherboard to get the on-board custom address and data chips to operate in the high resolution mode. I can't see any way of getting the on-board custom chips to operate in high resolution without making some modifications to the motherboard. You mentioned John Perkin's efforts.

What did he do? Perhaps a second set of custom chips and associated circuitry could be utilized as an add-on, but where would one get the custom chips from? Or perhaps the circuitry could be provided as an add-on and then the 3 on-board chips removed from their sockets and placed in their respective add-on sockets? It would be nice to come up with a simple means of providing any Astrocade user, how few there may be, the option of high resolution graphics, but it doesn't look like that's going to happen. Any comments?

Sincerely,
Michael C. Matte

3) Letter to Michael Matte by Bob Fabris (December 26, 1985) - Draft

12/26 [1985]

Dear Michael [Matte],

Your most interesting letter just arrived and I thought I'd best get back right away.  Primarily because there is no point in sending anything to Don Gladden.  He's not involved with Arcadian production any longer.

We'll certainly keep the Arcadian going for two more issues (I trust you received the December issue by now).  Whether to go after issues 3 and 4 depends on reader response and material to print.  It does seem like we have a somewhat dedicated kernel of Arcadian enthusiasts.

Balcheck II?  Now that's a big surprise!  Is Dick Belton aware of your efforts?  I'm sure he would find it very interesting.

And a high-rise machine too!  Motherboard changes are acceptable-- I recall John's board had lots of piggyback memory attached-- I'll try to get in touch with him-- I think he is still with?  We have some motherboards here and some spare chips as well.  Actually, the units themselves are getting so cheap that one can build up the extra parts relatively cheaply.

[Bob Fabris]

4) Hi-Res Package Cover Letter (to Bob Fabris) by Michael Matte (July 3, 1986)

July 3, 1986

Dear Robert:

Enclosed are five, what I have labeled as, "packages" for use as you desire.

I've thought about the possibility of production or sales for package 1 upgrade.  It would be great to play with games utilizing high-resolution graphics.  However, I see many complications.  I would be willing to make the necessary modifications to any motherboard and perhaps wire the power supply, but I have really little desire to wire wrap anymore RAM boards or audio/video boards.  Who would have the skills to layout and manufacturer a PC RAM board PC audio/video board?  Since much of the video RAM and composite video electronics was taken from the Datamax UV-1R computer, wouldn't permission be required from Datamax to market the RAM board and audio/video board?

What common means should be used to program the Astrocade high-resolution graphics: ZGRASS and/or a machine/assembly language monitor or BASIC?  I can't see how I could market any Hi-Res MLM [Machine Language Manager cartridge] if it utilizes portions of Bit Fiddlers' MLM, an Astrocade BASIC PC board, Astrocade BASIC routines for the audio interface (>=8000H constraint deleted) and routines almost identical to the Astrocade onboard subroutines?  DataMax utilized, at one time, 16K bytes ROM (including ZGRASS) for their UV-1 computer.  Perhaps this could be utilized into the upgrade.  However, the DataMax UV-1 computer required the use of a computer terminal.

What common means of saving data should be used?  Would an external keyboard be required?  Obviously, to get the most out of the high-resolution graphics, a common means of programming in that mode is required.  A group effort is indeed required to get the job done and maybe some input from potential users.  So tell me, is there a next step?  I need help on this one.  Who has the desire to invest in such a project?  Would there be enough interest to make the project feasible?

Recently, I read a Viper sales brochure claiming that their 8K/24K switch allowed any cartridges in the cassette slot to be copied out to Viper RAM.  This puzzled me.  Do you have any idea how this copy feature was accomplished?  I can see how the Z80 could read data from a cartridge and by electronic trickery, the same data would be written to RAM.  But this would require the user to utilize every aspect of the cartridge, so every byte of the cartridge would be read by the Z80. The 8K/24K switch in packages 1, 4 and 5 only allows the user to develop software addressed 2000-3FFFH with the intent that the software would eventually be realized in cartridge form.  That is, machine code can be entered/loaded into 6000-7FFFH and then switched to the respective locations in 2000-3FFFH.

Please explain your reference to Dick Belton, i.e. is he troubleshooting RAM add-ons?  What's his address?

As usual, please mail the enclosed postcard, so I know you received the enclosed material.

Sincerely,
Michael C. Matte

P.S. In case you're wondering, I spent much time developing the upgrade and Hi-Res MLM for my own use.  I also had the hope that more experienced people might take the upgrade and somehow market it and that I might act as an advisor or maybe even a partner.

--------------------

The hi-res Astrocade upgrade is very intriguing to me, and I figured who wouldn't want to read more about it from these letters.

Enjoy!

Adam
14544:
I have added details about the documentation that Michael Matte wrote about each part of his five "packages" in today's revamp of the Astrocade High-Resolution Upgrade area on BallyAlley.com.  Michael's documentation is handwritten, so I re-typed and used Dragon voice-to-text to create the descriptions, which (in most cases) are just slightly edited quotes of Michael's own descriptions of his "packages."

Hi-Res Package 1 - Astrocade System Upgrade

"Package 1" of the Astrocade System Upgrade (low or high resolution graphics, user RAM, composite color video output and audio output) contains fifteen pages of schematics and layouts. Here is what is included in Astrocade Hi-Res Package 1:

  1.  Contents
  2.  Modified Motherboard Schematic
  3.  Modified Motherboard Layout
  4.  Power Supply Schematic/Regulator Board Layout
  5.  Ram Board 50-Pin Contact Expand Interface Schematic
  6.  Ram Board User Ram Decoder Schematic
  7.  Ram Board User Ram Schematic
  8.  Ram Board Video Ram Interface Schematics (Two)
  9.  Ram Board Video Ram Schematic
  10. Ram Board Layout
  11. Ram Board Optional 16K Rom Decoder Schematic
  12. Ram Board Spares
  13. Audio/Video Board Schematic
  14. Audio/Video Board Layout

Drawing Comments

  1.  RAM Board Video RAM Schematic - Type 4116 dynamic RAM is used in lieu of type 4027, since it is generally cheaper and easier to obtain.
  2.  Ram Board Layout - Close To Actual Size
  3.  Ram Board Optional 16K Rom Decoder Schematic - Scheme Is Untested
  4.  Audio/Video Board Layout - Type LM377 audio amplifier chip is probably discontinued. Other audio amplifiers can be substituted. Radio Shack, for example, has several audio amplifier chips.
  5.  Audio/Video Board Layout - Close To Actual Size

Hi-Res Package 2 - Low/High Resolution Modification Procedure

Nineteen pages describing what and how to modify the Astrocade motherboard, plus how to wire the RAM board, which contains video and user RAM.

It is assumed the user of this procedure has a copy of the Bally Service Manual PA-1. Beginning experimenters in digital electronics should not attempt this upgrade. Several unused gate inputs are shown wired to +5V via a 10K current limiting resistor allowing TTL chips to be occasionally substituted in lieu of LS TTL chips. If only LS TTL chips will be utilized, then wire the unused inputs directly to +5V (no resistor). Numbers following procedure statements indicate reference should be made to the note numbers, which are listed following the procedure.

Two low resolution demos and a high resolution demo, for testing purposes, are available on cassette tape. Mail the request for the demos along with $7.00, to cover the cost of the tape, postage and packaging.


Hi-Res Package 3 - Copies of some Datamax UV-R1 Schematics

These schematics were used to come up with the Astrocade system upgrade package 1. Comparison of the schematics will show the similarities of the Astrocade upgrade with the Datamax UV-1R. For a complete set of Datamax UV-1R schematics and layouts (excluding power supply) contact DataMax Inc. I paid $30 for one set of prints (21 drawings). The notes on the attached Datamax schematics were added by myself, way back when I was for studying the schematics.


Hi-Res Package 4 - 44K Byte Dynamic RAM Add-On

This one-page instruction sheet uses three schematics in "Package 1 Astrocade System Upgrade" to make some deletions for this upgrade.

Add-on requires only +5V power supply. Refer to power supply schematic in Package 1. This add-on is recommended only for use with separate composite video and audio outputs between monitor/TV.


Hi-Res Package 5 - 12K Byte Static RAM Add-On

Static RAM does not require any refreshing or special timing circuitry. Data will remain intact as long as +5V is supplied to the board and the write protect switch is on. This feature allows the board to be disconnected from one computer and connected to a second computer or allow cartridge swapping without running loops. In either case, the data in Static RAM will remain intact (unchanged).

The Balcheck II display is optional and is used by Balcheck II software (not available at this time) to aid in troubleshooting the motherboard or static RAM. The videocade connector allows a videocade to be copied to tape. A videocade PC board, removed from its cartridge, is inserted in the videocade connector. Astrocade BASIC (or Bally BASIC) is then used to copy the contents of 6000-7FFFH to tape.

Incidentally, this add-on can be used with the Package 1 upgrade (connected to 50-pin expand header). This add-on requires only a +5V power supply.

------------------------------

I added a complete scan of Cavern Quest by Bruce Jaeger.  This program first appeared in Creative Computing 9, No. 7 (July 1983): 222, 224-225.  This scan was previously available, but it was missing the Vic-20 version of the type-in program.  The older scan was also lower quality.  This new scan are from the magazines pages that were torn from the original magazine and were in the Bob Fabris Collection.

"Cavern Quest" is a text adventure game that uses the joystick for input from the player. The game is large, random and pretty fun (if you map it!).

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#CavernQuestBASICType-In

I also took a screenshot of the game, which you can see here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#CavernQuestAB
14548:
I added the "AstroBASIC" version of Joe People's game Dot-to-Dot.  This was published in ARCADIAN 6, no. 4 (Feb. 23, 1984): 38.  This has never been available in AstroBASIC before.  I love to archive "new" programs!

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/joe_peoples/joe_peoples.html#Dot-to-DotAB

Joe submitted the "AstroBASIC" and Blue Ram BASIC versions of Dot-to-Dot together.  He wrote some instructions for this game over the course of two submission letters to the ARCADIAN (it seems the first submission letter was originally lost in the mail-- although maybe it just arrived late, as both letters are in the Bob Fabris Collection).  These brief instructions are based on what Joe wrote.

This is a two player game.  The object is to draw lines between two dots.  Try to complete a box to capture it.  Completing a box gives you another turn. Try to keep your opponent from being able to complete a box. To create a line, move the flashing dot to where you want to start your line and pull the trigger.  Then move the flashing dot to a dot above, below, to the right or left (no more than 1 done away and not in a diagonal direction) and pull the trigger.

Dot-to-Dot Archive Notes:

1) Paul Thacker compares Dot-To-Dot to the style of game that is similar to Claim Jumper from L&M Software.  Claim Jumper can be played as a one-player game (the computer will play the second player), but Dot-to-Dot requires two players.

2) In February 1984, this program was the prize winner for the best program of the month.

3) Dot-to-Dot is from the Bob Fabris collection. There were three copies on the tape. They aren't identical, but Paul doubts there are any code differences.

4) One of the two program submission letters for this program mentions that in addition to the tape containing two different version of Dot-to-Dot ("AstroBASIC" and Blue RAM BASIC), there is a third program called Horse Race Math.  BASIC, hand-written program listings for both versions of Dot-to-Dot were included in Folder 6-1 (Nov 29 1983) of the Bob Fabris Collection, but no listing for Horse Race Math was in it.  Interestingly, there is a program in the Bob Fabris Collection called Math Horse Race, but there is a handwritten note across the top of the hand-written BASIC listing that credits the program to "Lou Kleynen" (full name, probably Louis Kleynen).

I actually loaded this game in "AstroBASIC" so that I could take a screenshot of it.  It controls smoothly and run quite quickly.  I'll try to rope in Chris Federico to play a two-player game of this with me this week.

Thanks for archiving this program, Paul.

Adam

14550:
I added various documentation for several arcade games that use the Astrocade chip set.  This chip set is formally known in the Software and Hardware for the Bally Arcade (aka "Nutting Manual) as the "Midway Custom Circuits."  I think that all of the arcade games (Gorf, Wizard of Wor, etc.) use the Astrocade chip set.  The three custom chips are:

1) Data Chip (0066-116XX) - Component U18 in the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  This is the chip that gets very hot and is a common failure in the Astrocade console.  This chip doesn't overheat much in the arcade games because the custom data chip isn't locked-up tight inside RF shielding.

2) Address Chip (0066-115XX) - Component U17 in the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.

3) I/O Chip - (0066-117XX) - Component U19 in the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.

In a future episode of the Bally Alley Astrocast, I'm going to cover these custom chips and explain what each one does for our little Bally Arcade units.  Most tasks that the custom chips are capable of performing will work on the consumer unit (the Astrocade) except for the Rotator function, which only works in commercial mode (the arcade games).

In this post I'll mention the documentation that I uploaded for the 1980 arcade game, Extra Bases, which is a sequel to the 1976 game Tornado Baseball (which was ported to the Bally Arcade).

1. Extra Bases - General Instructions - One sheet of paper describing in general terms: Installation, Line Voltage Safety Switch, Voltage Control Pots, Volume Control, Service Control Panel and Align Ball Control Sensors.

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/Arcade_Games/Arcade_Games.html#ExtraBasesGeneralInstructions

14551:
I found Horse Race Math. It was on another tape in Bob Fabris's collection. A copy of Dot-To-Dot was on this tape as well. This tape was broken, so thanks to Chris for repairing it.
In Horse Race Math, up to four players solve simple math problems at the same time, with a correct answer making your horse move forward. There's no penalty for wrong answers. Try as many times as you want until you get it right. It's an interesting idea, but I did find it difficult to input such precise answers with the knob.
Enjoy this never before published Arcadian submission!
Paul

I have added HORSE RACE MATH by Joe Peoples to BallyAlley.com.  This is an unpublished ARCADIAN program submission from 1983.

Note: When Paul archived it earlier today, he labeled it as published is 1984.  That was the year of publication of Dot-to-Dot (which was submitted with HORSE RACE MATH).  Since this math game was never printed, I'm going with the original submission date of 1983 for this educational game.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/joe_peoples/joe_peoples.html#HorseRaceMathAB

Notes from Joe People's original submission letter:

HORSE RACE MATH is a rework of Howard Brecheisen's HORSE RACE program from ARCADIAN 3, no. 1 (Nov. 06, 1980): 6-7.  It's a 1 to 4 player game.  Use the Knob to get near the answer and then use the joystick (which disables the Knob until another program is displayed) to zero-in on the answer.  Pull the trigger when you have the right answer.  You can't hold the trigger and attempt to run over the right answer.  Note the arrays in the type-in program, which must be loaded without a line number.

Archiving Notes by Paul Thacker (July 9, 2016)

HORSE RACE MATH was on another tape in Bob Fabris's collection.  A copy of Dot-To-Dot was on this tape as well.  This tape was broken, so thanks to Chris Federico for repairing it.

In HORSE RACE MATH, up to four players solve simple math problems at the same time, with a correct answer making your horse move forward.  There's no penalty for wrong answers.   Try as many times as you want until you get it right.  It's an interesting idea, but I did find it difficult to input such precise answers with the knob.

Thanks for archiving this tape, Paul.  This program would have been lost if Chris hadn't have fixed the tape-- I'm glad that worked so well.  Thanks, Chris!

I added two Nitron catalogs.  For a time, beginning in, I think, 1982, Nitron built the Astrocade units for Astrocade, Inc.  These catalogs are part of the Bob Fabris Collection.

Some of the topics included in the catalogs include: Nitron Overview, Nitron's Place in the Industry, The Nitron Difference, Semi-Custom Design Concept, Nitrochip Design - Getting Started, Designing a Nitrochip, Questions and Answers, and much more information about the company and its products.

Nitron Catalog (November 1981)


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/nitron/nitron.html#NitronCatalogNov1981

Nitron Catalog (1982)


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/nitron/nitron.html#NitronCatalog1982

In "An Introduction to the BPA" by Bob Fabris, there is some background on Nitron:

"Early in 1982, Nitron of Cupertino, California became another player in the Astrocade group. In June, it became the principal supplier of hardware to Astrocade. In a rather unusual arrangement, Nitron bought Astrocade's entire arcade, cartridge and component inventory, contracting to purchase component parts (the major chips were sole-sourced from American Microsystems). Nitron then assembled the gear and sold it back to Astrocade. The purchase gave Astrocade some needed cash but made it highly dependent on Nitron's performance. Some Bay Area subscribers and I visited the facility and were impressed to see that Nitron apparently had all of the necessary equipment and capabilities to complete all of the required work under one roof (although the Garner and Sacramento plants were to continue their efforts, with Nitron as overseer)."

Maybe these Nitron catalogs can be used to help piece together the history of the manufacturing of the Astrocade in the 1981/1982 era.

I added the previously un-archived Metropolitan Attack! from ARCADIAN 6, no. 11 (Oct. 31, 1984): 110.  The author of this game is uncredited, but it was probably written by Dale Low.  You can download this game for "AstroBASIC" (and see a screenshot from it),  here:

This program appeared in the ARCADIAN newsletter with no author or instructions listed.  The game has not been found on any tapes, so I decided to type it in using TXT2PRG, KCS and 300 BAUD TO 2000 BAUD TAPE CONVERTER (from the "AstroBASIC" manual).

When the game runs, it looks very similar to the hand-drawn "screenshot" of Astrogames' METRO ATTACK on tape A1:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/reviews/Astrogames_Review/images/Astrogames%20Ad%20(Arcadian_vol_6_issue_4_page_032).gif

Yup, as can be seen from the above picture, this is a MISSILE COMMAND clone.

Michael Prosise reviews the game (briefly) in his December 1983 Game Player column:

"Metro Attack. Three cheers for Dale Low! This is a game I could really get excited about! It is the best MISSILE COMMAND simulation I have ever seen. It contains selectable levels, turns, players, bonus energy points, whew! In short, this game has it all! My personal favorite."

METROPOLITAN ATTACK! doesn't seem to have selectable levels or players, so maybe this program is slightly different from the tape release of the game.

Comments from Paul Thacker:

Thanks for typing it in. It seems to work well, and is a solid game on top of that.

Having read everything I could find on METRO ATTACK by Astrogames, which is a surprisingly large amount, I think METROPOLITAN ATTACK is almost certainly by Dale Low / Astrogames, but I tend to think that it's a different version. Here are some differences:

1) The Niagara review says it has selectable levels, turns, and players, but the only thing you select in this is the number of bases (lives).

2) The Arcadian review in volume 6, page 7 (which also calls it "METRO ATTACK
1988", presumably predicting a nuclear war in a few years) says you shoot from five bases, but this one only has three. But maybe that's an error in the review, since it does draw five bases. Or even a bug in the code. Hard to say.

3) It's advertised as using machine language routines in Arcadian volume 5, page 172, and Niagara page 12. I don't see anything like this in the printed code in the Arcadian listing.


Archiving Notes, by Adam Trionfo

Here's some additional information about METROPOLITAN ATTACK! And some of the archiving process:

1) Load the game with :INPUT;RUN

2) I spent some time figuring out how to make a title screen using the article "Title Screen Instructions" from the April 1983 Arcadian newsletter.  This is pretty time consuming... but it works.  I don't know if I'll do this again for other programs.

3) The game handle controls your missile cursor and the trigger fires a missile.  The Knob controls from which base you shoot (left, middle, right).
This works pretty well, so my guess is that using the division sign on line 100 was correct.  The only downside is that there is no indication from which base you'll be shooting-- you have to get used to the position of the knob to know your firing-base location.

4) You can run out of missiles from each base, so you do need to shoot from different bases.

5) If you score around 400-600 points than you get a bonus base (life) and you get a fuel bonus (but I don't know what that is-- maybe it is points... I didn't notice).

6) When the game is over, then you exit back to BASIC.  This is normal, as I checked the program's flow.  You can restart the game from BASIC without issues.

This is a pretty good game-- certainly one of the more fun type-in games that I've seen.


Enjoy!

I added four previously unarchived video art programs and one unarchived game by Dieter Heinerman to BallyAlley.com.  These five programs were all originally published for Bally BASIC in the Arcadian.  I have converted the Bally BASIC, 300-baud versions of these programs to "AstroBASIC" using Jay Fenton's 300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Converter from the "AstroBASIC" manual.  However, no changes were made to the original Bally BASIC programs.  Therefore, the sound in these programs may not work properly due to differences in the way that BALLY BASIC and "AstroBASIC" handle the sound ports.  Also, as with all "AstroBASIC" programs, these programs run faster in the newer version of BASIC.  This gives the video art programs more of a "rushed" feel that they didn't have in their original format.


The five programs that I've added are:

I)   Added a video art program called 3D Corners by Dieter Heinerman.
This program appeared in ARCADIAN 3, no. 4 (Feb. 07, 1981): 49.

1. 3D Corners - (Bally BASIC, 300-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#ThreeDCornersBB

2. 3D Corners - ("AstroBASIC," 2000-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#ThreeDCornersAB


II)  Added a video art program called Boxes by Dieter Heinerman.  This program appeared in ARCADIAN 3, no. 4 (Feb. 07, 1981): 49.  On the program submission tape, this program was called RND Boxes.

1. Boxes - (Bally BASIC, 300-Baud)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#BoxesBB

2. Boxes - ("AstroBASIC," 2000-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#BoxesAB


III) Added Denominator by Dieter Heinerman.  This program appeared in ARCADIAN 3, no. 4 (Feb. 07, 1981): 49.


Denominator is based on an article called Extended Precision Computation by Stephen Rogowski that explains "how to compute to a practically unlimited number of places with just the memory your micro has on board." The original article appeared in Creative Computing 6, no. 3 (March 1980): 94-95.

1. Denominator - (Bally BASIC, 300-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#DenominatorBB

2. Denominator - ("AstroBASIC," 2000-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#DenominatorAB


3.  Extended Precision Computation by Stephen Rogowski (article in pdf format):


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/Denominator/Extended%20Precision%20Computation%20(March%201980)(Stephen%20J%20Rogowski)(Creative%20Computing).pdf

IV)  Added a video art program called Electronic Blanked by Dieter Heinerman.
This program appeared in ARCADIAN 3, no. 4 (Feb. 07, 1981): 49.

1. Electronic Blanked - (Bally BASIC, 300-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#ElectronicBlankedBB

2. Electronic Blanked - ("AstroBASIC," 2000-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#ElectronicBlankedAB

V)   Added the game Defuse by Dieter Heinerman.  This program appeared in ARCADIAN 3, no. 5 (March 7, 1981): 58.  This game was originally published in More BASIC Computer Games, by Creative Computing, Edited by David H. Ahl. 1979: 48.

In this game, you are in an experimental building with one million rooms in it. The building is one hundred rooms long, one hundred rooms wide, and one hundred rooms high.

You have just received a telephone call from a mad bomber who tells you he has planted a bomb someplace in the building. Fortunately you are armed with a bomb detector that registers a stronger and stronger signal as you get closer to the bomb. You start at the bottom right-hand door of the building, at the room 0,0,0. In response to the signals from your detector, every ten seconds you may try a new room to search for the bomb. You have two hundred seconds or twenty trials to find it.

1. Defuse - (Bally BASIC, 300-Baud)


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#DefuseBB

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#DefuseAB

3.  Defuse, original listing in More BASIC Computer Games, by Creative Computing, Edited by David H. Ahl. 1979: 48.


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/Defuse/Defuse%20(1979)(More%20BASIC%20Computer%20Games).pdf


These five programs took a long time to archive.  Finding background information, testing, snapping screenshots , converting each program from Bally BASIC to "AstroBASIC" and making sure to include any fixes (when necessary) was time consuming... but fun!


As I said a couple of days ago when I archived Diamond, there is just something, I don't know, magical about video art programs running on the Bally; I just love watching them!  I think it's because each one of these video art programs is just that, a work of art by an individual.


Check 'em out and... enjoy!

I have added Greg White as the author for Bally Trek, a Bally BASIC program that was archived from the Bob Fabris Collection.  Paul and I discuss a letter by Greg's father, Joe, in the Bally Alley Astrocast #4.  Joe mentions that his son, Greg, is working on a game.  This game is Bally Trek, which is based on Erik Mueller's Star Trek for MINOL - Tiny BASIC.


I found the instructions for this Bally Trek in the Bob Fabris Collection.  I OCRed/re-typed them and have added them to the archive (as well as to this post).  I also took a screenshot of this game.  You can download Bally Trek here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#BallyTrekBB


Here is the November 26, 1978 letter to Bob Fabris where Joe mentions Bally Trek:


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#JoeWhiteLetterNov261978


After taking a look through the Bob Fabris Collection, it seems that the archived version of Bally Trek was probably submitted with a letter that Joe sent to Bob on January 20, 1979.  This letter isn't yet available on BallyAlley.com.


@Paul: Since Slot Machine was on the same tape as Bally Trek, do you suppose that Greg White also wrote that game?


Here are the instructions for the Bally Trek:


BALLY TREK
By Greg White
1979

Sample Display:

.*..K..1      CONDITION RED
K...*..2      TIME LEFT 3O
*..E..*3      SECTOR 3,4
K....*.4      ENERGY 1000
..*....5      KLINGONS 15
*...B..6
..*..*.7
1234567

UNIT HIT FROM KLINGONS 75
COMMAND? 1
X-COORDINATE? 1
Y-COORDINATE? 5

In the above display the commands that may be
entered after COMMAND? are:

     1 is entered for phaser to kill Klingon.
     2 is entered to move Enterprise in quadrant.
     3 is entered to move Enterprise to another
       quadrant to find a Starbase or more Klingons.

After X- or Y-COODINATE? enter a location 1 through 7.

To refuel, dock Enterprise above or below a Starbase

In the display:

     E equals Enterprise.
     B equals Starbase.
     * equals a star.
     . equals a blank space.
     K equals a Klingon.

Object of the game is to destroy all Klingons before
running out of energy or time. When low on energy try
to find a Starbase. There is not a Starbase in every
quadrant. Whenever a phaser is fired, Klingons score
a hit, or the Enterprise is moved, energy level
is lowered.

You will receive a message if a Klingon is destroyed; if
you run out of energy or time or if you miss a Klingon.


Did anyone here play these text-only versions of Star Trek?


Enjoy!


Adam

14600:
I added Speed-O Math by Bob Wiseman.  This is a previously unarchived program was printed in Arcadian 3, no. 1 (Nov. 06, 1980): 6.

The Arcadian's directions for this game are very short, "This math drill program uses the giant letter routine."  You can download the program here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_q-z/programs_q-z.html#Speed-OMathBB


This program is referred to as Speed O Math in the Arcadian newsletter, but Bob Wiseman's original program submission calls it Speedo-Math.  I deferred to Bob's original program name.


I've transcribed Bob's original submission letter:

October 9, 1980

Dear Robert Fabris (Publisher),

I was pleased to see that you are continuing the ARCADIAN for another year. My
check is enclosed.

Over the course of 1979, you published three of my programs. It gave me great
joy to see my work in print. I even received a fan letter from a fellow YAHTZEE
addict. I agree that the dice should have been larger. I wrote the program
while in Canada and had no available machine. My Trinitron resolved the dice
tolerably well, and I was generally too busy playing to correct the situation.
Ah well, one of the joys of the machine is snipping here, pasting there... Let
someone else enjoy himself.

I enclose a cassette with two offerings on it. I give you the right to publish
these in the ARCADIAN as you see fit.

On side one there is a short program that uses the "giant letter" routine. This
is a math drill program that I call SPEEDO-MATH. All input is through the
keypad.  If your subscribers modify this very much, the letters will have to be
moved higher on the screen to avoid wiping out the program.

On side two I have included my version of MASTERMIND. The computer holds a four
color code. Try to guess it. Enter the first letter of each color through the
keypad. Each black is a correct color guessed in the correct spot. Each white
is a correct color in the wrong spot. I wrote this from scratch.

I wish you well on your endeavors with the Bally. I think that a machine
language monitor in the Blue-Ram would be a worthwhile project. I have tired of
waiting for a Bally add-on. I bought an Apple-II Plus in February and am very
pleased with my purchase. I am now writing a series of machine language
animation games that I hope to market.

Thank you again for your good work on the ARCADIAN. Could you please publish
how many subscribers there are? Perhaps you could draw more advertisements?

Sincerely,
Bob Wiseman

You can read the letter in its original scanned form, here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#LettertoBobFabrisByBobWisemanOct091980

Enjoy!

Adam

I added a previously unarchived game called Bally 500 by Bob Hensel to BallyAlley.com.  This was published in Arcadian 3, no. 5 (March 7, 1981): 56-57.



Here are the instruction from the Arcadian:

"Bally 500 is a game of driving skill for 2 or 3 players. One player controls the turns in the road with KN(4). The other players control the cars with KN(1) and KN(2). Road blocks, accidents, and other cars are randomly placed in your path. If you hit one, then your car is destroyed. The object is to see how long you can stay on the road, and beat your opponent. An elapsed time is indicated at the top-left of the screen. Skill Level: 3 (hard) - 10(easy)"


You can download Bally 500 here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#Bally500BB


The instructions say that the game can be played with 2 or 3 players, but for practical reasons, three players are required. This is because there are always two cars racing, even if one isn't controlled by a player. When a car crashes (by driving off the road, then the game ends for everyone. So, while technically the game can be played with as little as two people-- the game will last for only a few seconds before the other car crashes.  Or... am I overlooking something...?


Have fun!


Adam

10 PRINT "HELLO WORLD

After along conversation with Mike White about the screen saving of the AstroBASIC program, he said that the screen shares it's memory with the BASIC program 1 bit at a time. This means that 1 bit is program, the next is pic the next is program, pic, program, pic, etc. don't know which one comes first, the chicken or the egg, Then there is the problem of knowing exactly how the other software stores it's info. I'm sure that all of the programs such as Paint, PDF, PING, TIFF, IMG, etc. all do it their own way. You'd have to pick 1 out of the many and have someone like Mike Garber or Richard Degler come up with a translation program that can put into extended memory something that Repack can use. Sounds like a huge can of worms to me.
Ken

14612:
Can the 300-baud interface be powered by an external power supply?  If so, how?


Adam
14613:
the power pins for the 300 baud interface are on the Light Pen jack. The one closest to the hand control port is the +5V and the one towards the outside is the ground. Any good USB sourde can be rewired to do the job. HOWEVER, the light pen's middle wire is used for signal. So defeating the original supply will still require a wire to the center pin.Ken

I have added background material for Jay Fenton 1982 "game" Life.  This program has been archived on BallyAlley.com for many years, but this past weekend Paul Thacker pointed to me that Byte magazine has an issue dedicated to Life.  I noticed that the manual for Fenton's Life "borrows" much of it's information (including illustrations) from this magazine.


George Moses sold Jay's program.  Ads for Life are here:

Arcadian 4, no. 12 (Oct. 07, 1982): 122.
Arcadian 5, no. 2 (Dec. 3, 1982): 35.

Here is what the ad says about Life:


"Sure, you've seen seen Life games before. A BASIC program was published in a magazine a year or two ago. It took 5 or 10 minutes per generation! Well, how about one generation per second? Yup!!! Jay Fenton, the guy who wrote Bally BASIC, Gunfight, Scribbling, Calculator and Gorf has revved-up you Z-80 processor to give you a full screen scan and a new LIFE generation each second! Put some LIFE in your Arcade (and give some spending money to Jay Fenton to keep him in "programming mode!"). Buy Life and Get Nuke the !$&! free!"

The manual for Life and Get Nuke the !$&! is available here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/tape_manuals/misc/Life%20and%20Nuke%20the%20---.pdf


The December 1978 issue of Byte magazine has many articles dedicated to Life. While none of these articles/programs are specific to the Bally Arcade/Astrocade, the manual for Life does directly lift quite a bit of material.  You can read the entire issue (or just browse through it) on archive.org:


https://archive.org/details/byte-magazine-1978-12


Thanks for the tip to Byte magazine, Paul!

14617:
I added five letters to Bob Fabris or Bally Home Library Computer customers from various Arcadian readers or JS&A National Sales Group.  Paul and I discuss each of these letters on the upcoming Bally Alley Astrocast #4.

1) Added December 27, 1978 letter to Bob Fabris from Jim Unroe.


Jim canceled his order with JS&A after waiting for long time and then he got an Arcade unit right away from another dealer (yes, even at the end of 1978, JS&A wasn't getting enough units from Bally to fill orders).


He's having issues with his unit (it sounds like overheating). He notes that you can have commands executed directly from tape rather than being loaded as a program line. This is one advantage of Bally BASIC over "AstroBASIC." Jim talks about wanting to create an elaborate alarm system using his Bally Arcade.


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#LetterJimUnroeDec271978


2)  Added January 22, 1979 letter to Bob Fabris from Glenn Pogue.


Glenn says that if a user complains about the unit's name change, then Bally will send a "tag" to those users who request one that says "The Bally Computer System." This letter has a list of release dates (month and day) for Bally games, including some that were never released at all (including Checkers, Desert Fox, and Astrology).


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#LetterGlennPogueJan221979

3)   Added January 22, 1979 letter to Bob Fabris from John Sweeney.

John requests Executive Software by Tom Wood because he is trying to write an assembler for the Bally Arcade. This is very early in the Bally Arcade's history to be working on something like this.  There is no evidence that this assembler was created, but General Video Assembler (which required a RAM expansion) was eventually written and released on tape in 1982 by Dave Ibach and Steve Walters (General Video).  Dave used this assembler to write his centipede-inspired, cartridge game, Sneaky Snake.

John talks about safe places for assembly code in Bally BASIC (he uses the editor/buffer).  He recommends some articles/books for Tiny BASIC information.

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#LetterJohnSweeneyJan221979

4)  Added January 29, 1979 letter to Bob Fabris from Guy McLimore.


Guy is a Bally Arcade dealer for ABC Hobbycraft.  Guy has popped up on the Bally Alley Yahoo group from time to time.  In this letter, Guy says that he gets more information from the Arcadian newsletter than he can get from Bally-- and he's a dealer!  He mentions several programs he's working on.  He suggests that Bally should make a second, more detailed (I presume) version of the Bally BASIC manual for "the really rabid Arcade freak."  (I love that term!) In a way, Jay Fenton's Hacker's Manual was this second "book," but it was only about twenty pages long and probably wasn't widely available.  Too bad that there isn't a book called Compute!'s First Book of the Bally Arcade.


This letter gives a different perspective on Bally providing information to users. It seems like maybe they were willing to tell anyone inquiring what they knew, but for something like the add-on, they just didn't know what they were going to do yet (or ever!).  Also, the add-on seems to be proposed to sell for $650, but JS&A advertised it for $300 in their original Bally Home Library Computer ad in September 1977.


Guy mentions his Dungeon Grafix programs. These may have been the first D&D programs for the Bally Arcade.  Guy also mentions a Star Wars-inspired program.


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#LetterGuyMcLimoreJan291979


5) Added May 1979 letter to Bally Arcade customers from Joseph Sugarman.

Joe Sugarman, the president of JS&A, claims that the company "had spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in advertising to obtain our sales."
That's a lot of money, which makes it hard to believe this claim.

However, in the early 70s, when JS&A began, full-page ads in the Wall Street Journal cost about ten-grand (says Joe in his 1980 book, Success Forces), so perhaps this high-dollar advertising figure is possible.

Joe seems to basically be giving up on the Bally system.  He offers quite a few options for people to get refunds or special offers on other JS&A products (for instance, getting a portable TV, worth more than the Bally, for an even trade if you don't want to continue to wait for your Bally Home Library Computer).  Joe also offers to allow people to return the system a year later, which is pretty generous (certainly more than is required), but he doesn't go as far as offering a cash refund.


Joe is clearly willing to throw Bally under the bus at this point (arguably deservedly). Bally hasn't announced a cancellation of the add-on expansion, but he predicts (correctly) that it will never come out.


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/jsa/jsa.html#JosephSugarman51979


I used some notes that Paul Thacker sent to me (thanks, Paul!) to create these summaries of each letter.  The summaries only touch upon the very basics of some of what the letters contain.  To get a better understanding, Paul and I discuss some of these letters in much more detail in the podcast, but even there we don't cover any of the letters from start to finish.  If these letters interest you, then read them in their entirety.  You're sure to...


...have fun!

Adam

14621:
I archived (on BallyAlley.com) a December 11, 1978 letter to Bob Fabris from Brett Bilbrey.  Paul and I discuss this letter in the upcoming Bally Alley Astrocast #4.

Brett was a mainstay of the early issues of Arcadian and Cursor. He went on to write two Astrocade cartridges (ICBM Attack and Treasure Cove), contribute to the "AstroBASIC" manual and work for Action Graphics (as well as contribute to the Bally community in many other ways). Later, Brett worked for Apple.

When this letter was written, Brett was attending the University of Michigan. He talks about building his own printer (which no longer worked). He lists six BASIC programs he wrote (or, possibly, co-wrote): Strek Trek, Shoot, Life, Life for Two, Simon and Othello.

Brett makes some comments on Space Race. It was originally going to be paired with the Clowns and Brickyard, but then developed into what looks like Star Battle.

This eight-page letter shows a hardcore user's enthusiasm for the Bally Arcade.


You can read the letter here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#LetterBrettBilbreyDec111978


Have fun!


Adam

Wow... That letter brought back a flood of memories...

 This letter was when I first started playing with the Bally Arcade. It was just before I started reverse engineering the hardware and ROM. I had just jumped into 'electrical engineering' (as my degree) and was learning a ton.
 

 I was such a geek. (OK, I still am.)
 

 But this was before I saw the Nutting manual. I had to figure out on my own what all the 'peek and poke' commands did. This was shortly before I wrote the 3 voice music player.  As you can see from the puzzle at the end of the letter, I love brain teasers, puzzles and games.
 

 Brett

Brett wrote:
>>
Wow... That letter brought back a flood of memories...
>>

I hope that all these memories that flooded back were good ones.

I really love exploring the letters that people wrote to Bob Fabris at the Arcadian.  There is so much locked-up computer-culture history inside those letters.  Even though most people wrote specifically about their Bally Arcade system, the computer history that they talk about can be broadly applied to many of the early 8-bit platforms.  There are certainly more similarities between early computer adapters than differences.

>>
First, I did not 'write' the Star Trek game. I either typed it in from the book "101 basic games" or one of my friends that I started Spectre System with did it. (That is true for all of the games listed. Star Trek, Shoot, Life, Life for two, Simon, Othello)
>>

Okay, that makes sense.  Thanks for pointing that out.  I'll have to figure-out some way with Paul to properly credit these games (@Paul: any ideas?).

I just realized that Star Trek (the text game) has its own Wikipedia entry:


https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_(text_game)

The 1978 released of BASIC Computer Games: Microcomputer Edition by David H. Ahl, can be bought rather cheaply on Amazon.com:


https://www.amazon.com/BASIC-Computer-Games-Microcomputer-David/dp/0894800523

The book's illustrations alone are worth the price!  If you don't own this book, then you should get it.  However, pdf versions of the book are available from many places online.  Here is a direct link to Super Star Trek, the game upon which (I suppose?) that the Bally version of Star Trek that Brett sent to Bob is based upon:


http://annarchive.com/files/Basic_Computer_Games_Microcomputer_Edition.pdf#page=172

Yesterday, I just watched an episode of the original Star Trek for the time in many, many years.  The episode I watched was "Patterns of Force" (the one that has the world with Nazis on it).  Two things about the show struck me.  First, all of the special effects were redone (what?!?).  Here is a side-by-side example of the changed special effects from "Space Seed:"


https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3WGhvS2LGTM


Second, the writing on Star Trek still holds up today.  I'm not sure I like the redone special effects, but it probably does make the show more accessible to a younger generation of fans.  After all, Star Trek is fifty years old now.  Yikes!


>>
I had to figure out  on my own what all the 'peek and poke' commands did.
>>

Brett wasn't the only one who was doing his  best to figure-out how the Bally ticked.  Some people did it with an educated background (as Brett did), and others tried to find their own way by semi-randomly POKING as many locations as they could and noting the results.  The Arcadian (and Cursor) was an essential resource for all the people who were experimenting with the Bally console.

>>
I was also working on seeing  how many colors I could display at once. (Which  I incorporated into my cartridges later...)
>>

Yes, Treasure Cove is without a doubt the most colorful game on the console.  It's also jolly-well fun to play today.

As for colorful programs, "Display All 256 Colors on Screen at One Time" by Jerry Burianyk is an interesting case.  This was originally published in CURSOR 2, no. 5 (January/February 1980): 87-87 (it was later included as a type-in program in the "AstroBASIC" version of the manual).  Part of the description from the program's first printing says, "The 256 color program uses Screen Interrupts which Brett Bilbrey so brilliantly pioneered with his CRITTER program in the October 1980 issue of CURSOR."

Thanks for being an original fan (fanatic?) of the Bally Arcade in 1978, Brett.  It's wonderful that you still frequent this Astrocade group!

Adam

14627:
I've been trying to plug the holes lately in the archived program collection for teh Astrocade.  Over the last couple of days,I was getting frustrated with archiving some of the programs from the Arcadian and Cursor that are on "tape."  Many of them just won't archive for me.  I'm thinking about throwing them in Paul's direction, as he's the archive expert.  However, in the meantime, to take a break from trying to archive the "tapes," I've worked on some other programs using other archiving methods:

Typed in:

1) RND (Art)  - Super Software - Typed it in.  This will be available in BB and AB.

2) Slot Machine - Al Roginsky - I actually OCRed this program-- it doesn't really save any time (it might even take MORE time)-- but it was worth trying.  I must proofread this one still.  This will be available in BB and AB.

3) Tycoon - Alex Morales - Typed-in this Cursor program. I still must proofread this one.  This will be available in BB , but I'm not sure how compatible it will be with AB.

Archived from tape:

4) NEW GHOST [Revision] - This is a revision of HALLOWEEN GHOST by James Wilkinson, originally printed in ARCADIAN 2, no. 10 (Sep. 17, 1980): 103-104.  This will be available in BB only.  I'm not sure if I'll add this to the HALLOWEEN GHOST archive as an alternate version (the code is VERY different).


5) POP ART - This was printed as CIRCLES in ARCADIAN 3, no. 7 (May 08, 1981): 77.  I'm not sure if this will run correctly under AB-- certainly the sound won't work right.

6) PICK A PATTERN - Unpublished Arcadian submission that was previously unavailable.  I'll only archive the BB version.

Archived from tape and Typed-in

7) RING - By Albert Paul - This Cursor program on tape was significantly different from the printed version, so I modified it to be the original version too.  Both the original and the alternate version will be available in BB and AB.

The programs that I archived from tape came from these two files:

1) New Ghost, Pop Art Pick A Pattern by Dr. Daley (300 baud)(raw).wav - contained NEW GHOST.

2) New Ghost, Pop Art Pick A Pattern by Dr. Daley (reverse) (300 baud)(raw).wav - Contained POP ART and PICK A PATTERN.

It looks like I'm getting quite a lot done, BUT...


...my BIG set back was the failure of my main Astrocade this morning.  First it wouldn't run the 300-to-2000 Conversion program properly, then it started crashing and then the sound went wonky.  All this within a couple of minutes.  So, of course, I shut it off.  At least it didn't Halt and Catch Fire, right?

I switched over to my alternate Astrocade machine, which works okay, but the keyboard is stiff and the debounce on it is pretty poor.  Hopefully this one will last awhile.  Wouldn't it be great if there was an easy fix for these nearly 40-year-old machines?


I wish that Astrocades held up the way that Atari 2600s hold up to this day.  Then again... if Astrocades did hold up well, then we might be playing on the Bally Arcade 4 instead of the Playstation 4.  (Yeah, wishful thinking-- I'd be glad just to get the add-on/add-under/ZGRASS system).

This means that 1 bit is program, the next is pic the next is program, pic, program, pic,  etc. don't know which one comes first, the chicken or the egg, Then there is the problem of knowing exactly how the other software stores it's info. I'm sure that all of the programs such as Paint, PDF, PING, TIFF, IMG, etc. all do it their own way. Sounds like a huge can of worms to me.

Ken

the power pins for the 300 baud interface are on the Light Pen jack. The one closest to the hand control port is the +5V and the one towards the outside is the ground. Any good USB sourde can be rewired to do the job. HOWEVER, the light pen's middle wire is used for signal. So defeating the original supply will still require a wire to the center pin.
Ken

14634:
Actually, Mike White and I did a lot of research into the amount of current that the cassette interface used, so that we did not exceed that amount. We actually came in about 20mA less, but that was just because we used less and more modern CMOS chips. Tha interface does bring the total current very close to it's upper rated limits. However, the majority of the current consumed by CMOS chips is only when they change states, from on to off and vice versa, so it is only momentary.There is a chance that a power supply circuit has parts that are right at teh edge of the tolerance and could be struggling with the 300 BAUD interface, but it shouldn't cause catastrophic failure unless a chip shorts out.There are several inputs to the interface. an oscillator keeps it in sync with the unit, the input and the output, as well as the power.
Check Arcadian Volume 1 No.3 page 20. There is a lot more than just the light pen connected.Ken

That's what I suspected by reading the Bally Basic source code. The light pen interrupt is probably used for precisely timed tape input, or as sort of a switch: the tape interface may generate a reference interrupt frequency, so the Astrocade uses the interrupt vector to sample the input and for outputting the signal on tape recording.
In case the light pen interrupt is only used as a clock reference, the actual input is probably done via the controller connector, no surprises here. The only strange thing is that the controller port is also used as an output - that may help to explain why a very specific one is required: it's probably hardwired to the chips in a way it can be used as an output.
I wish I had the wiring information for the interface. Looking at the schematics only I'm not sure about where each connection goes to or comes from.
