the power pins for the 300 baud interface are on the Light Pen jack. The one closest to the hand control port is the +5V and the one towards the outside is the ground. FOX AND HOUNDS written by Dan Drescher of Esoterica Limited, is a checkers-type game. You get 4 pieces located at the bottom of the board, and the Computer gets one piece at the top of the board. The game object is to box the Computer into a corner eliminating any further moves. You may only move forward on black squares. Computer may move backward. Differences between tape and BASIC type-in versions:

The two versions are identical except for these four differences:

1) The tape version has this direct command before the program loads: CLEAR ;&(10)=0

3) Line 9 of the program in THE BASIC EXPRESS does not have the closing quote mark.

      170 if TR(1)if PX(P,L+3)=00if PX(P-3,L+3)=1goto 600

Following the first equal sign, there are two zeros.  It should probably be only one (as in the BASIC listing in the newsletter).

14638:
I added PICK A PATTERN by Ron Picardi.  This is an unpublished ARCADIAN submission from either 1980 or 1981.

PICK A PATTERN allows you to make your own patterns, which works... but I don't really know how to choose options that make good patterns.  The random element (option 2 on the menu) makes some of the most random, ultra-cool video art that I've ever seen on the Bally system!  I let it run for a while now and I snapped pictures of the coolest-looking output.

You can download the original 300-baud Bally BASIC version of PICK A PATTERN here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/Ron_Picardi/Ron_Picardi.html#PickAPatternBB

The AstroBASIC version is here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#PickAPatternAB

It's too bad that Ron Picardi didn't simplify this program and eliminate options 1 and 3, which require LOTS of user input.  This probably would have made the program publishable (and much shorter in length).  As it is, it stands, I believe, as one of the most interesting (probably THE most interesting video art program) on the Bally (in either published or unpublished format).  The only issue that I have with it is that some of the art it makes takes a long time to finish.  This is because it's totally random for how many iteration each drawing cycle runs.  I guess that's also part of the beauty of the program.

Ron included rudimentary instructions on how to use PICK A PATTERN with in his program submission letter.  Although Ron's documentation may seem long, they are basic on the details:

Design your own computer art.

Menu

1. Design
2. Random Pattern
3. Squares

0 Returns to menu

Random pattern is programmed by the computer.
Design and Squares are user-programmed.  The user would need to play with this to figure out what it does.

Design

1) 60 to 60 step?
2) 30 to 30 step? Try 10 or 20
3) For 1 to?
4) Box?
5) Step?
6) Repeat?
7) Step?

3-7 - Try various numbers from 1-30.

Color - Input a number from 0 to 32
8) FC
9) BC

Music? 1 or 0 (Yes or No)
1 GO 1 Reset 1 Runs Program When done 0 Menu 1 repeats 2 gives a print out


Squares

1) FOR 1 TO ? - Try 30
2) STEP ? - Try 2 to 5
3) BOX? - Try 30
4) STEP - Try 2 to 5

1 - Single Box - Will do one square
2 - 2 Boxes - Will do two squares
3 - Rectangle - Will do one rectangle

Music? This sets &(20) FC - Input from 0 to 32 BC - Input from 0 to 32

When the program is over, E appears.
Input 1, or 2 or 3.  This will re-RUN the boxes to mix your pattern.  Any other input returns to menu.

Have fun designing.

In this simulation, you manage a small factory that produces three different kinds of products (P1 - P3).  Three different kinds of raw materials (R1 - R3) are required to produce the products.  Each product requires exactly two raw materials with a different subscript.  For example, to manufacture one unit of P2, you would need a unit of R1 and a unit of R3.  To manufacture one unit of P3, you would need a unit each of R1 and R2.

There are two levels of play in this simulation.  The range of costs and prices for level 2 will be in parentheses.

The cost of raw materials varies from $10 to $20 ($10 - 30) per unit.  It costs from $1 to $9 ($1 - 20) per unit to manufacture a product from raw materials.
The selling price of each finished product varies from $50 to $90 ($40 - 104) per unit.  Prices of raw material and manufacturing costs will vary by not more than $3 ($5) per turn.  Prices of finished products will vary by not more than $6 ($10) per turn.

You will receive a data report at the beginning of each turn.  This report will give you the number of units you have on hand, available cash, and the manufacturing cost.  You can buy (B), manufacture (M), sell (S), or do nothing (0) each turn.  In order to manufacture a given product, you must have enough of the correct kind of materials on hand.  If you make a mistake in ordering you will lose a month's transaction.

You can manage this factory monthly for up to 36 months in 12 month increments.
After your time has expired, the materials and/or products that you have on hand will be automatically sold at the current prices and your profit will be computed.

ITEM  MATERIALS  PRODUCTS

  2     0@$18      0@$78
  3     0@$18      0@$72
MONTH  0  YOU HAVE $ 500
MFG. COSTS ARE $2
TRANSACTION (0,B,M,S)? B

I found one more unique program on this tape--Horserace by Paul Slezak. This is already on-line, but that version came from Richard Houser's Arcadian compilation tapes (and should be named as such). This version exactly matches the newsletters. Here are the differences.
Line 410 has "A#49STOP" in the newsletter. The version currently on-line has "A#4STOP". This is checking if you pressed the 1 key. My testing indicates that the newsletter got it right.
Lines 50 and 60 are also different.

Newsletter:
50 CY=-32;print "PLAYER #",;print #1,Z,;CX=-20;input B;CY=-32;CX=10;input C
60 if B>0if B<10goto 80

Currently on-line:
50 CY=-32;print "P #",;print #1,Z,;CX=-47;input "CHOICE"B;CY=-32;CX=10;input "BET"C
60 if B>0if B<9goto 80It's pretty subtle, but otherwise I wouldn't have realized that the version Richard Houser made didn't match the newsletter exactly.
Paul

    I added Speed-O Math by Bob Wiseman.  This is a previously unarchived program was printed inArcadian 3, no. 1 (Nov. 06, 1980): 6.

This program is referred to as Speed O Math in the Arcadian newsletter, but Bob Wiseman's original program submission calls itSpeedo-Math.  I deferred to Bob's original program name.

I've transcribed Bob's original submission letter:

October 9, 1980

Dear Robert Fabris (Publisher),

I was pleased to see that you are continuing the ARCADIAN for another year. My
check is enclosed.

Over the course of 1979, you published three of my programs. It gave me great
joy to see my work in print. I even received a fan letter from a fellow YAHTZEE
addict. I agree that the dice should have been larger. I wrote the program
while in Canada and had no available machine. My Trinitron resolved the dice
tolerably well, and I was generally too busy playing to correct the situation.
Ah well, one of the joys of the machine is snipping here, pasting there... Let
someone else enjoy himself.

I enclose a cassette with two offerings on it. I give you the right to publish
these in the ARCADIAN as you see fit.

On side one there is a short program that uses the "giant letter" routine. This
is a math drill program that I call SPEEDO-MATH. All input is through the
keypad.  If your subscribers modify this very much, the letters will have to be
moved higher on the screen to avoid wiping out the program.

On side two I have included my version of MASTERMIND. The computer holds a four
color code. Try to guess it. Enter the first letter of each color through the
keypad. Each black is a correct color guessed in the correct spot. Each white
is a correct color in the wrong spot. I wrote this from scratch.

I wish you well on your endeavors with the Bally. I think that a machine
language monitor in the Blue-Ram would be a worthwhile project. I have tired of
waiting for a Bally add-on. I bought an Apple-II Plus in February and am very
pleased with my purchase. I am now writing a series of machine language
animation games that I hope to market.

Thank you again for your good work on the ARCADIAN. Could you please publish
how many subscribers there are? Perhaps you could draw more advertisements?

Sincerely,
Bob Wiseman

You can read the letter in its original scanned form, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#LettertoBobFabrisByBobWisemanOct091980
Enjoy!

Adam

I added the Bally BASIC program Lace Curtain by Fred Cornett.  This was printed in Cursor 1, no. 3 (March 1980): 21.  I also added a screenshot of the program running.


The program is part of a brief tutorial that explains how to use Port 9 (horizontal blanking register) and Port 10 (vertical blanking register). Included is short example program, Lace Curtain, that displays four colors at once using a complicated-looking, but eye-pleasing, pattern.

You can download Lace Curtain (which has the tutorial in text format as part of the archive), here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html#LaceCurtainBBFredCornett


Note: I converted Lace Curtain to "AstroBASIC" using Jay Fenton's 300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program.  The program seemed to work okay, but there was "trash" (garbage) in the upper-right corner of the screen (only on the right side of the horizontal color boundary).  I've noticed that this happens on some programs under "AstroBASIC" that directly access some of the Ports.  Because of this possible compatibility issue, I've decided not to digitally archive this program in "AstroBASIC."  Can anyone take a look at the program (below) and see what might cause this issue?

Here is the complete tutorial:

Screen Format Output Ports

If you wish to put more than 2 colors onscreen simultaneously (while using TINY BASIC) without resorting to machine language, it can only be done by formatting the screen. Port "&(9)" is the "Horizontal Blanking Register." By setting this port to various values, it will do a number of things:

1. Vertically split the screen
2. Put up screen borders

Input this program example:

10 FOR A=0TO 256;&(9)=A;PRINT A;NEXT A

The Color Ports are as follows:

Ports &(0) through &(3) control the colors used on the Right side of the screen (in conjunction with the use of &(9)).

Ports &(4) through &(7) control the colors used on the Left side of the Screen (in conjunction with the use of &(9)).

To use these ports, you assign them values just as you assign values to FC or BC.

Look at lines 5 and 6 of the following program, and you will see how to assign value to these ports.

NOTE: "&(10)" is the "Vertical Blanking Register." Substitute &(10) for &(9) in the above one line program to see how it works


LACE CURTAIN

5 BC=10;FC=83
6 &(2)=0;&(1)=53;&(0)=53
10 CLEAR ;&(9)=148;FOR A=-79TO 79STEP 2;BOX A,0,1,87,1;NEXT A
20 FOR A=43TO -43STEP -2;BOX 0,A,159,1,1;NEXT A;FOR A=1TO 100;BOX 0,0,RND (159),RND (87),3;NEXT A;RUN


The preceding program puts up 4 colors at the same time. By changing the value of &(, you will get 5 colors. Try experimenting!


Note: The above paragraph was hard to read, I think that "&(," is supposed to say "&(10)," but I can't be sure.


Have fun!


Adam

.STANDBY for :return ;:input 2
>null {2}.GOLF -BY BOB HENSEL
.ALL GOLF RULES APPLY
.JX(1) for BALL ANGLE
.JY(1) for CLUB 1 to 9
.TR(1) to HIT THE BALL

.input # OF PLAYERS
:return ;NT=0;BC=25;FC=92;&(0)=170;&(1)=170;&(2)=7;&(3)=7;input N;&(9)=20;goto 100

"Bally 500 is a game of driving skill for 2 or 3 players. One player controls the turns in the road with KN(4). The other players control the cars with KN(1) and KN(2). Road blocks, accidents, and other cars are randomly placed in your path. If you hit one, then your car is destroyed. The object is to see how long you can stay on the road, and beat your opponent. This is because there are always two cars racing, even if one isn't controlled by a player. When a car crashes (by driving off the road, then the game ends for everyone. So, while technically the game can be played with as little as two people-- the game will last for only a few seconds before the other car crashes.  Or... am I overlooking something...?

Have fun!

14653:
I have added a version of Golf by Bob Hensel that has brief instructions included on the "tape."  This game was originally printed in Arcadian 3, no. 4 (Feb. 07, 1981): 46-47.  A correction was printed in Arcadian 3, no. 5 (Mar. 07, 1981): 51.

You can download the Bally BASIC version of this program, here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#GolfBobHenselBB

"Golf is a game of skill for 1 to 4 players. The computer generates 9 different holes each game, randomly placing each green and hazards such as tress, water, or sand traps. Each player selects the direction the ball will travel by moving JX(1) until the rotating line points in the proper direction. The distance is dependent on the club selected using JY(1). Remember the flight of the ball is affected by the direction and velocity of the wind."

When this game starts, it prompts the user for N.  I think that this is asking for the number of players (1-4).  Certainly entering "1" will give a one-player-only game.


Thanks for archiving this game (and instructions), Paul!


(We've been adding lots of Bally programs lately-- all right!)

Adam
14654:
FIY, My Arcade Golf 1.5 was started from this program with Bob Hensel's permission. I just made the ball flight, the moving of the golfer, the hole sink and thr "hole in one" routines were all mine. I just was able to use the Blue RAM BASIC to create the 4 colors displayed as well as the ability to do "faster and more detailed" graphics. I also made it 4 player with the ability to select hand controls and # of holes. It can be found on all of my UltiMulti carts but is only playable with extended memory.Ken

14655:
While doing a search today for some Astrocade-related material, I came across an early version of the Bally Alley website.  This is from so long ago that it wasn't yet BallyAlley.com, as it was hosted on the Game Spy network (remember that wesbite?).  Here is a link to Bally Alley, as it looked in May 2003:


http://archive.kontek.net/ballyalley.classicgaming.gamespy.com/


The Bally Alley website moved to a new (non-GameSpy) server in September 2004.  At the point where the site is archived (in the above link), there still weren't even any programs available for download yet... which is little weird because programs had begun to be archived in about the summer of 2002.  Certainly, Bob Colbert had begun writing the tools required to convert tapes back then.  On March 12, 2001, in a post titled "Ballywav Progress Update," Bob wrote:

"I just thought that I would post an update on my progress in writing the ballywav/blly2wav/astrowav (any preference on the name) program. Actually, my first step is going the opposite direction, that is from a .wav file to a .bin file (blly2bin)"

You can read the complete post, here:


https://beta.groups.yahoo.com/neo/groups/ballyalley/conversations/messages/71


I think the BallyBin/AstroWAV tools first became available in an early form in the Spring of 2002.  "AstroBASIC" 2000-Baud programs, in the early days of archiving, were still considered to be test cases.  For this reason, it took me quite awhile to trust the archive tools enough to add them to the Bally Alley website.


It's also very strange to think that there was a time when any tape/program archiving was done without Paul Thacker.  His first post, entitled "Greetings, " to the Bally Alley Yahoo group was May 27, 2005.  Paul didn't mess about though, for he soon began wondering about tape archiving.  Just a few days later, on May 31, Paul posted a message titled "Tape Arching," where he wondered:


"I am curious about the state of Astrocade tape archiving. Obviously many tapes have been recorded and are available at BallyAlley.com, and will hopefully eventually be supported by an emulator. However, I've also seen many programs mentioned that I don't think are available on the site. It is difficult to be sure, though, since it seems many programs could be released on a single tape. [...]  Has anyone ever made a list of unarchived games? Is there any effort to save them from the inevitable ravages of time?"

One of Paul's hopes in this early post was that the MESS emulator would eventually support tapes.  Well, we're still waiting for that little upgrade to the Astrocade emulator in MAME!


Paul must have been visited by the tape archiving bug, because before long, Paul was getting tapes and archiving them.  It's safe bet (I think?) to say that the Astrocade's archived tape software library would be just a sampling of its current state if Paul had not happened to have got involved in the system (by discovering it via emulation in MESS).


It's weird to think how long I've been playing around with my little Bally Arcade.  The system was born in the late seventies, it came into my hands in the mid-90s, and its heart still beats loudly to this day!  Viva La Bally!

Adam

14659:
>>
I never knew that you could tap into the calculator by using the $ command. It probably could have made some calculations much easier to do.
>>


This feature only works in Bally BASIC.  This feature was removed from "AstroBASIC."  To put it a bit comically, Jay Fenton comments, "The interface to 16 digit BCD math calculations ($ command) has been kicked out."  This is noted (with many other changes) in Jay's New and Improved BALLY BASIC document:


http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/new_bally_basic.txt


There weren't many programs that used this feature, but those few that did could be rewritten in an Expanded BASIC, for those improved BASICs kept this feature.

Adam

I've archived a tape in the Bob Fabris collection by an unknown author. Adam found the tape and some related source code in a folder with material from 1979. The tape is labeled with Craps, Slots, and Bowling. I also found a fourth program which has a brief audio introduction that sounds to me like "Preposition F". Of course, I'm not actually sure what that means. Craps also had an audio introduction.
The games are pretty simple. Bowling has the ball move back and fourth automatically, and you pull the trigger to throw it. There is no other input, so no spin or anything. There is also no scoring, and the game seems to go on forever.
For Slots, you enter how much money you start with, then it plays automatically until you run out of money.
For Craps, you enter a wager, and it automatically rolls the dice for you until the round is over.
I'm not really sure what Preposition F does. You enter a number and it does some calculations and  then prints out some letters.
I really wanted to figure out who wrote these, but I still can't say with any confidence. I looked through the software list to see if any possibilities stood out. I believe the closest match if Steve Walpole, who offered to sell source code for Computer Craps and Slot Machine in Arcadian Volume 1, issue 10, page 84. He isn't known to have made a bowling game.
Scott Waldinger actually wrote Craps, Craps 2, Slot Machine, and Bowling. But we have source code for Craps 2 and Slot Machine, and I don't see any similarities. But it's possible that he made a lot of changes between the versions of Craps, and that there are multiple versions of Slot Machine as well.
Ron Schwenk wrote Craps, which we don't know anything about, but not the other games to my knowledge.
John Collins and W&W Software both wrote bowling games in 1979, but they don't look like this one.
David Stocker, Bob Mueller, Ernie Sams, Robert Strand, and W&W Software all wrote slot machine games in 1979, but they don't look like this one.
(Wow, there are a lot of slot machine programs on the Astrocade!)
Any other ideas for identifying these?
Paul
14666:
Are you mainly looking for personal reflections on playing the game? Here are some stream of consciousness thoughts on the game. Please edit for clarity:
Incredible Wizard had some of the best sound effects for a game from that era and was a lot of fun to play. It was the game that got me into playing games and while I was never really good at the game, I really liked the fact that this game had radar to help track the monsters and played and felt like a real arcade game. The only other home version that came close was the Commodore 64 version.
This game is very well suited for the Astrocade controllers. Incredible Wizard is one of the best games to play from the pre-1984 era of videogames. I would rank it easily in my top 20 from that era.

Are you mainly looking for personal reflections on playing the game? Here are some stream of consciousness thoughts on the game. Please edit for clarity:


Incredible Wizard had some of the best sound effects for a game from that era and was a lot of fun to play. It was the game that got me into playing games and while I was never really good at the game, I really liked the fact that this game had radar to help track the monsters and played and felt like a real arcade game. The only other home version that came close was the Commodore 64 version.


This game is very well suited for the Astrocade controllers. Incredible Wizard is one of the best games to play from the pre-1984 era of videogames. I would rank it easily in my top 20 from that era.

This game sold the game system to me back in the day! When I was a kid I was on a bowling team and there was a small arcade at the bowling alley. One of the games there was Wizard of Wor. It was one of my favorite games along with New Rally X and Donkey Kong Jr.  Needless to say, when I saw this game in Montgomery Wards. I was blown away with the graphics and sound. At the time it was the most true to the original coin-op as any other game system had. It was that moment I told my parents what I wanted for Christmas. The Bally did not have the most games but they had a few games that were must have in my mind during that era.

Adam

14676:
David,


As far as real hardware goes, your multicart sound "legit."  I've done business with RetroKidz and never had any trouble.  Hacked accounts do happen from time to time.  I'm glad to hear that you're getting some of your money back.  When you get your multicart, I hope that you find the time to update your feedback.


Sadly, it doesn't appear that your Demo cart is Muncher.  The picture that you attached to your post is actually the Bally Arcade Demo cart.  When it's plugged in, it basically shows the Bally playing the built-in software and then plays some music.  It's pretty neat, and it is rather hard to find, so you did all right from a buying perspective... but it's just not the Pac-Man clone that you hoped to get.


When you picked up your Astrocade, did you still have the tapes with the programs that you created?  If so, then I'd love to see them archived on BallyAlley.com.


Mark's uncle was referring to Jay Fenton who is now Jamie Fenton.  Jay programmed some of the built-in ROM software, as well as programming Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC.  He also created the arcade game Gorf and many other interesting software projects.


You said "back in Chicago on the PBS station WTTW [...] I remember watching an indy film called “Skippy Peanut Batter Jars” [...] at the end of the short, in the credits it had said Images Produced by Bally Astrocade Zgrass Computer."


Since you lived in Chicago, I imagine that this movie/video was programmed on the ZGRASS systems that were available in the computer lab at the University of Chicago.  Tom Defanti, the designer of ZGRASS, worked there.  The school's art program actually used ZGRASS systems, and students created "artsy" videos that seem very similar to what you describe.  Perhaps this "Peanut Butter" video was created by Jane Veeder, Phil Morton or Copper Giloth-- three prominent students from about that era.


Here's an example of a video (called "Evil Meat") that was created on the ZGRASS system in 1984:


https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vw2ebTkROBs


If you search YouTube for "ZGRASS," then you'll find some other videos too.


Adam

I know I have some tapes, I can go through them.  I have a second system I got at a garage sale a few weeks ago, it had some tapes as well.  Ya know, there was this user group in Chicago that had this crazy idea... Evatone sound sheets. They were flimsy sheets of plastic that were in magazines, or direct mailers or even cereal boxes, flimsy super cheap "records".  They were trying to get some made that had the 300 baud programs on them. They could be produced for about a quarter and then you would go home and record the record to a tape , and then load the tape. A great idea since Tapes were much more expensive. They were trying to put programs for a zine called cursor, and I had one with a PAC man game called rat maze, or mouse maze, something like that. I could never get it to load, so I typed it in one day...  But kinda a rare form of media distribution.   I also remember sending my unit in to some place to be modded, heat sinks added, better connector on the power plug, some other stuff. As far as real hardware goes, your multicart sound "legit."  I've done business with RetroKidz and never had any trouble.  Hacked accounts do happen from time to time.  I'm glad to hear that you're getting some of your money back.  When you get your multicart, I hope that you find the time to update your feedback.
Sadly, it doesn't appear that your Demo cart is Muncher.  The picture that you attached to your post is actually the Bally Arcade Demo cart.  When it's plugged in, it basically shows the Bally playing the built-in software and then plays some music.  It's pretty neat, and it is rather hard to find, so you did all right from a buying perspective... but it's just not the Pac-Man clone that you hoped to get.

When you picked up your Astrocade, did you still have the tapes with the programs that you created?  If so, then I'd love to see them archived on BallyAlley.com.
Mark's uncle was referring to Jay Fenton who is now Jamie Fenton.  Jay programmed some of the built-in ROM software, as well as programming Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC.  He also created the arcade game Gorf and many other interesting software projects.
You said "back in Chicago on the PBS station WTTW [...] I remember watching an indy film called “Skippy Peanut Batter Jars” [...] at the end of the short, in the credits it had said Images Produced by Bally Astrocade Zgrass Computer."
Since you lived in Chicago, I imagine that this movie/video was programmed on the ZGRASS systems that were available in the computer lab at the University of Chicago.  Tom Defanti, the designer of ZGRASS, worked there.  The school's art program actually used ZGRASS systems, and students created "artsy" videos that seem very similar to what you describe.  Perhaps this "Peanut Butter" video was created by Jane Veeder, Phil Morton orCopper Giloth-- three prominent students from about that era.

Here's an example of a video (called "Evil Meat") that was created on the ZGRASS system in 1984:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vw2ebTkROBs
If you search YouTube for "ZGRASS," then you'll find some other videos too.
Adam

Mark's uncle was referring to Jay Fenton who is now Jamie Fenton.  Jay programmed some of the built-in ROM software, as well as programming Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC.  He also created the arcade game Gorf and many other interesting software projects.

You said "back in Chicago on the PBS station WTTW [...] I remember watching an indy film called “Skippy Peanut Batter Jars” [...] at the end of the short, in the credits it had said Images Produced by Bally Astrocade Zgrass Computer."

Since you lived in Chicago, I imagine that this movie/video was programmed on the ZGRASS systems that were available in the computer lab at the University of Chicago.  Tom Defanti, the designer of ZGRASS, worked there.  The school's art program actually used ZGRASS systems, and students created "artsy" videos that seem very similar to what you describe.  Perhaps this "Peanut Butter" video was created by Jane Veeder, Phil Morton or Copper Giloth-- three prominent students from about that era.

Here's an example of a video (called "Evil Meat") that was created on the ZGRASS system in 1984:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vw2ebTkROBs

If you search YouTube for "ZGRASS," then you'll find some other videos too.

Well, if I could have easily made a track ball controller, I would have.  

 The reason I picked a 'joystick' was it was the closest thing I could do that would inexpensively simulate a trackball.
 

 The process I used to design the controller was by finding an existing joystick that had the same resistance (or close) to that of the hand controller knob. (I don't remember what that is off the top of my head.)
 

 I added the two pinball buttons on either side. They were the hand controller 'trigger' contacts.
 

 For the 'digital' joystick on the bally handle (that is, moving the knob front to back, and left to right...), I connected those lines up to the 'phone keyboard'.
 

 I had not thought about 'hacking' a Vectrex controller, but that might be possible.

Dear Arcade Fanatic:

The enclosed half-page advertisement was xeroxed from today's Minneapolis Star and Tribune. The nationally-known firm of C.O.M.B. (Close-Out Merchandise Buyers), well-known advertisers in Popular Mechanics and other such hardware jock mags, has acquired a 1.2 million dollar stash of 1982, fresh-in-the-box, Astrocades. Figuring a street value of $240 bucks apiece (AstroBasic not included), this adds up to an inventory of 5000 machines. And they are for real...I drove over to C.O.M.B. and checked them out myself. The price: 98 bucks apiece! Now, you and I both know that is well below dealer cost, and damned close to what it cost Astrocade to market the things. And who would have a stock of 5000 of them just lying around? Most dealers I know talk in terms of dozens... never thousands. The only clue we are given is that they were acquired from "...a financially troubled East Coast distributor...". Don't forget that C.O.M.B. is making a few bucks on this deal themselves; they didn't buy them for anything near the 98 dollars each that they are selling them for. Somebody took a bath somewhere... we can smell the soap all the way up here in Cold Country.

I am sending this note to you for several reasons. First, you are one of the key people in the Arcade underground and can be trusted to either spread the word like wildfire or figure out a way to cash in on this action yourself; I don't care which. I'll run interference for anyone who needs help, since C.O.M.B. is a Minneapolis firm, but I won't put up any front money this time or crate up units and run back and forth between UPS and C.O.M.B. Tornado Baseball/Hockey/etc.
Demo Derby/Grand Prix
Biorythmns
Dogpatch
Red Baron/Panzer Attack
Brickyard/Clowns
Galactic Invasion
Space Fortress
Astro Battle (Space Invaders)
That dippy Star Wars down-the-trench thing
...and about six other old titles.

No, they don't have The Incredible Wizard, or anything newer than Space Fortress.

Good luck, you Arcade nuts, and I hope somebody is happier about this than the guy on the East Coast that lost his pants. (5000 units...that's got to be, like, Sears or Montgomery Wards. Nobody stocks 5000 Astrocades. Nobody stocks 5 Astrocades that I know of.)

Oh, yes, my now-famous closing line: Sounds like the end to me. But I've been saying that for four years now. Who the hell is Nitron, anyway?

Your pal,
Craig J. Anderson

Bally BASIC Demo, by Bally Mfg. Corp. - Functional Series - 8K cart - 1978. This cartridge has a small (about 6") chain attached to the top-front. This cartr...


On real hardware, if you were to run the Bally BASIC Demo cart again, then it would be a little different because the video art sections of the demo are random.  Neat, right?

Here's what Mike White wrote about this cartridge in the Bally-Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ:


Bally BASIC Demo

By Bally Mfg. Corp.  Functional Series              8K cart  1978.


This cartridge has a small (about 6") chain attached to the top-front. This cartridge was made in limited quantities and only distributed to dealers, as was also done with the Dealer Demo cartridge. This 8K cartridge ( a rarity in the old days) is very hard to find, but has appeared on eBay. The first 4K is a "crippled" version of Bally BASIC that doesn't have access to the keypad or hand controllers- except #3: all the inputs are disabled. The remaining 4K of the cartridge is a program written in BASIC! This was in 1978, EIGHT YEARS before Basicarts appeared! This cartridge may have sometimes been accompanied by a 300 Baud Demo Interface. This cartridge might be #6003 (it fits there), but there is no proof of this part number assignment.  (Arcadian 1, no. 6 (May. 4, 1979): 39-46.)


Back in 2001, Mike White sent me a print-out of the BASIC program that is contained on the Bally BASIC Demo cartridge:


http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/bally_basic_demo_cart.pdf

For those that are curious, I captured this video from an Astrocade equipped only with RF-out.  The RF-out was fed into my Ambery "Professional RF Coax To Composite Video Audio Demodulator TV Tuner For NTSC System" (model RFDM2).  I highly recommend this clever device.  You can buy it here:

http://www.ambery.com/prrfcotocovi1.html


I plugged the composite output of the Amberly demodulator into the Hauppauge! HD PVR model 1212 and captured the video as 720x480 at 30fps using Hauppauge! Capture.  I then trimmed the M2TS video to its current length using the freely distributable Videopad by NCH.  I exported the video (as an mp4) from Videopad, in the process trimming some of the overscan area that was originally captured.  The final exported video is 640x480, and it looks pretty good considering that the video is plain RF and not true composite or S-Video.


As for this BASIC demonstration that one may have seen running in stores in 1978/79, it only shows the most rudimentary features of BASIC.  Realistically, what more could you expect in 1978?


Now that I've been able to capture video, maybe I'll learn how to make a video review.  That's something that I've wanted to try doing for quite a few years.  I've always wanted to review Bally BASIC with the tape interface and also review "AstroBASIC."  Maybe I'll do that over the next few months.

Adam

14696:
I have successfully used Lance Squire's BIN2BML PERL script to convert the Bally BASIC version of Andy Guevara's Standard Color Generator to "AstroBASIC."  This "AstroBASIC" machine language program can now be loaded using the :RUN command from BASIC.


I don't think Paul or I (or anyone?) has ever archived a program using this method before now.  BIN2BML was originally created to convert binary images to 2000-baud format for use with expanded RAM so that a program in expanded RAM could run for the $2000 cartridge area .  However, I figured the tool might work just as well for the small 128 byte programs required by the :RUN command.  Once I changed the original Bally BASIC program to run from "AstroBASIC" (it wouldn't have RUN otherwise), BML2BIN worked like a charm.

You can download BIN2BML here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/tape_archive_tools/tape_archive_tools.html#Bin2BMLLanceSquire


The ability to use this conversion program is intriguing.  I was able to go directly from a source code file assembled with the Z80 assembler Zmac to the final 2000-baud program that loaded directly via "AstroBASIC."  Sure, there were a number of intermediate steps required, but it did work.  This proves to my satisfaction that someone could write a small game in machine language that would run from "AstroBASIC."


As an aside, a would-be machine language programmer wouldn't be limited to a 128-byte program-- but I think that's all :RUN can handle without a custom loaded being created.


Pretty neat, right?


(Thanks for writing this PERL script, Lance!)

Adam
14697:
I have added two utility programs to BallyAlley.com: :RUN MAKER and STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR.  Neither of these programs was available on tape, so I typed them both in myself (one last night, and one today).  I used TXT2PRG to type in :RUN MAKER.  After archiving :RUN MAKER, I ran it on a real Astrocade so that I could type-in and save the 300-baud version of STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR.

The "AstroBASIC" version of STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR was created from the re-typed source code.  I had to change one jump location so that the ML version that run under "AstroBASIC" would return to BASIC correctly after finishing this.  I wouldn't have been able to figure this out if the source code of both Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC wasn't readily available.  Archiving these three programs was pretty involved, but I learned how AstroBASIC can be used to run ML programs.  I also learned some new archiving techniques (which I'm sure will come in handy in the future).

:RUN MAKER will only work under BALLY BASIC.  It is available here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html#RunMakerBB


STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR is available in Bally BASIC, here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html#StandardColorGeneratorBB

The AstroBASIC version of STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR is available here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/cursor_basic-express/cursor_basic-express.html#StandardColorGeneratorBB

Here is the full article (and program listings ) from the BASIC EXPRESS newsletter for both of these programs :


:RUN MAKER / STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR
By Andy Guevara
BASIC EXPRESS, THE 3, no. 2 (May/June 1981): 15-16.

One of the least documented features of BALLY BASIC that I've seen is the :RUN command to input machine language programs from tape. Nowhere is the information on how it works to be found!! Being primarily a machine language type, I felt it was time to puzzle it out of the BALLY BASIC disassembly listing.

Basically, what the :RUN command does is open the tape input port and throw whatever characters come in into memory starting at address 4000 Hex (16384 Decimal), which is the first byte of screen RAM. As it loads, you can see it making tracks across the top of the screen. It continues to load bytes (by a happy coincidence an ASCII character with parity is 8 bits long) until an internal counter says stop, which it does after 128 bytes have been loaded. At this point, an immediate jump is executed to address 4000 Hex and the loaded program starts. Unfortunately it is 128 bytes, no more, no less, meaning shorter programs have to pad the ending with zeroes. Longer programs will have to incorporate the loader and direct the loading to another area in memory.

What the following program does is allow a machine language program, coded in Hexadecimal, to be input and stored on tape. Once stored, all you gotta do is :INPUT and run the tape. Your program starts by itself.


STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR

The "Standard Color Generator" program listed following the :RUN MAKER will display a series of color bars which can be used to set the colors on your TV set. When entering this example, DO NOT enter the addresses (i.e., 4000:). They are shown only for reference.

After you have keyed in the :RUN MAKER, press RUN and GO, then fill in the HEX codes as stated in the "STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR" listing, IN ORDER, by pairs, followed by GO. If finished before 128 has been entered, key-in "xx" (mult. signs) to stop the input mode. For example, the "STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR" ends with pair #69. Zero-padding to #128 is done automatically by the program.


If you find a mistake too late to use the ERASE key, you can still recover by hitting the HALT key, then typing in the following:

FOR N=##TO 128;G0T0 20

where ## is the number of the offending byte (make sure you type this line in without a line number!!).

Notes.....

A couple of notes: The ERASE key does work, but only on the current byte and looks a little funny in operation. Pressing the ERASE key will start the current byte over, placing it to the right of your original entry. Also do not be disturbed by what the Bally puts on the screen as it writes to the tape port... most of the HEX codes are not displayable as ASCII characters. The program works because the tape port gets data before the Bally Basic screen routines get a chance to change it all to "?".

LAST NOTE: When running your machine language program (such as "STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR"), don't let the cursor drop so far as to cause the screen to scroll, as this will cause the program to scroll right out of memory as well. If your cursor is approaching the bottom of the screen, you can pull it up by keying in a "CY=0".

The machine language program can be stopped by typing :RETURN, and restarted by typing CALL 16384.

:RUN MAKER - BASIC Listing

Archiving Note: This BASIC listing is in the format required by the 300-baud archiving utility TXT2PRG by Ronaldo Goulart.  For example, keywords are lower-case and some symbols that aren't available on a personal computer keyboard are replaced with keywords.  Notably, the multiply sign (x) is replace with "mul " in the text below.  This listing was typed-in and then converted to a WAV file using both TXT2PRG and KCSWIN.

3 clear
5 for N=1to 130;@(N)=0;next N
10 print "INPUT HEX CODE, mul mul =STOP
15 for N=1to 128
20 print N,":",
25 A=KP;TV=A
27 B=KP;TV=B
30 if B=31goto 20
35 C=KP;TV=C;if C=31goto 20
36 if C#13goto 200
40 if (A=98)+(B=98)goto 100
50 C=A;gosub 250;if F=0goto 200
55 A=Cmul 16
60 C=B;gosub 250;if F=0goto 200
70 @(N)=A+C
80 next N
100 print ;print "START RECORDING...HIT ANY KEY WHEN READY
110 A=KP
120 clear ;NT=1;:print ; print ".";print ".
125 print "clear
127 print "CY=20;:run
130 for N=1to 130
135 for N=1to 130
135 for A=1to 10;next A
140 TV=@(N)
150 next N
155 clear
160 :return ;print "DONE
180 STOP
200 print "ERROR
210 goto 20
250 if (C<48)+(C>57)mul (C<65)+(C>70)F=0;return
255 F=1
260 if C<65C=C-48;return
270 C=C-55;return


STANDARD COLOR GENERATOR

Archiving Note:  There is one error in this program on the line that reads "11 14 06  .LD DE,0C14H ; XY POSITION." 14699:
This week I've been typing in some BASIC programs from CURSOR/THE BASIC EXPRESS newsletter.  Two of the programs that I wasn't sure were archived were Bio-Rhythm and Moon Landing.  It turns out that what I thought was an alternate version of a CURSOR newsletter actually contains the instructions and BASIC listings for the two games.


The following are the docs and BASIC listings for Bio-Rhythm and Moon Landing.:


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/cursor/cursor_1980.pdf


Both of these programs were archived from tape by Paul.  You can download and play these 300-baud programs in BALLY BASIC:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/Sebrees_Computing/Biorhythms%20&%20Moon%20Landing%20(1980)(Cursor%20and%20Sebree's%20Computing)(300%20baud).zip


It's a good thing that the tape was available, because the BASIC listing for MOON LANDING is so small it's impossible to make out properly.


After examining the BASIC listing of MOON LANDING, I saw that it has a machine language portion.  The BASIC listing doesn't say what it is, which made me curious.  I looked at the contents of the tape, and I converted the Bally BASIC ML data to hex and then disassembled the code mostly by hand (with a little help from the DZ80 disassembler).  Converting the graphics of the lunar lander took some time, but was kinda fun to figure-out.


Here the disassembly of MOON LANDER (I'm not sure how well it will come-out here-- you can always copy and paste this section into another document):


; MOON LANDING
; Machine Language Subroutine at $4EE8 (20200 decimal)
; By Tim Hays
; Copyright April 1980 by Seebree's Computing
;
; Disassembled by Adam Trionfo with dZ80 2.0 on September 1, 2016
;
; This is a disassembly of the machine language code that is loaded
; from tape after the BASIC portion of the MOON LANDER program.  This
; routine prints the lunar lander graphics and explosion.  The ML
; portion also contains three graphics of the lunar lander (facing in
; three different directions) plus one explosion.
;
;  Special Memory Location used by BASIC program:
;
;       $4E70 (20080 decimal) - Memory location of variable B
;                               Variable B holds the location of the
;                               STRing DISplay subroutine.
;       $4EEB (20203 decimal) - STRing DISplay, X-Coordinate
;       $4EEC (20204 decimal) - STRing DISplay, Y-Coordinate
;       $4EF5 (20213 decimal) - Character to print: $80-$83

        INCLUDE "HVGLIB.H"      ; HOME VIDEO GAME LIBRARY

        ORG     $4EE8           ; 20200

; ****** Start from BALLY Basic with CALL20200 ***
;        Variable 'B' is set to 20200 when the tape loads.  Thus, the
;        BASIC program CALLs the STRing DISplay routine with CALL B
;        The BASIC portion of MOON LANDER changes the X and Y
;        coordinates by changing addresses $4EEB (20203 decimal) and
;        $4EEC (20204 decimal)

L4EE8:  PUSH    DE               ; Save Basic Program pointer
        SYSSUK  STRDIS           ;  UPI STRing DISplay
L4EEB:  DB      $1B              ;  ... X-Coordinate = 27
L4EEC:  DB      $00              ;  ... Y-Coordinate = 0
        DB      $28              ;  ... Options = 40
        DW      $4EF2            ;  ... String Address = 20210
        ;

14700:
Last night, I showed my friend Chris the work I did on disassembling the Display String machine language subroutine in Seebree's Computing's MOON LANDING .  I had not played the game since Paul archived it (maybe even before then-- as it seems to have been 10 or so years since I've seen this game).  I loaded-up MOON LANDING and Chris and I played a few rounds of it so that I could better explain to him what I meant about the machine language routine being seen right on the screen.

MOON LANDING has two game screens.  The first screen is the typical lunar landscape with several places to land your craft.  Different point values are awarded depending on how difficult it is to touch down on a landing pad.  On the second screen, you must re-dock with your "MotherCraft."  It's this second screen that I want to talk.  After a bug I encountered, I was surprised that the game was released AT ALL without a fix being made for this docking screen.

As is typical of any Astrocade game released for BASIC or on cartridge, you can never allow the game's graphics to overwrite the screen area where ML routines are stored (typically BASIC places ML routines at the bottom of the screen).  Also, graphics must never overwrite the screen where variables are stored (cartridges usually store variables at the bottom of the screen).  Since nearly 100% of the RAM on the Astrocade is screen RAM, you can easily overwrite ML routines and/or variables if you're not careful.  For example, in BASIC, if the screen scrolls... then any machine language routine stored onscreen will be wiped out.  This setup requires careful planning to use ML routines from BALLY BASIC or "AstroBASIC."

Some people have an understandably difficult time fathoming storing machine code or variables on the screen.  It may seem weird.. well, let's admit the truth: it IS weird.  Using screen RAM was a cost-cutting measure that allowed the Bally Home Library Computer to ship at a reduced price.  It wasn't as though Bally was doing anything that the rest of the industry at the time was avoiding.  For instance, it was also due to cost-cutting measures that made Atari shipped the VCS with 128 bytes of RAM.  The Bally's 4096 bytes of RAM may seem exceptionally large compared to the Atari 2600's miserly 128 bytes of RAM, the reality is that most RAM on the Bally system can't be used for variables or code: screen RAM must be devoted to what the user wants: graphics for games.

Whatever amount of RAM that you devote to machine language code or variables reduces your vertical screen resolution.  On the Bally home system, every 40 bytes of RAM that you dedicate to RAM reduces your screen area by 1 line of vertical resolution.  For example, the native resolution of the Bally system is 160 (wide) x 102 (high).  That gives you a maximum screen resolution of 16,320 pixels.

I'm not aware of ANY game that uses the full-screen resolution of the Bally Arcade.  As an example, both BALLY BASIC and "AstroBASIC" use RAM at the bottom of the screen.  This is why the maximum screen resolution of BALLY BASIC is reduced to 160 x 88 (14,080 screen resolution).  This 14-line vertical reduction in resolution gives BASIC access to an additional 560 bytes of RAM (14 lines x 40 bytes = 560 bytes) which it uses for strings, BASIC variables, the tape buffer and simply running an a BASIC interpreter.  Luckily, BASIC makes sure that the user can't easily write over this hidden portion of RAM at the bottom of the screen.  That's not to say that a user CAN'T write over this portion of RAM-- it's just not easy to do without resorting to machine language.

The Bally is extremely flexible with how you can reserve certain areas of RAM for the program... but the programmer MUST take care of this himself.  If the programmer isn't careful, then the program can crash quite easily.  That's the issue with MOON LANDING-- the programmer just wasn't careful: there's a game-ending bug.  I wish I could give a reason for this, as the game seems to be programmed quite cleverly, and quite a few tricks are used to get the maximum benefit from BASIC.  Yet, somehow, the game shipped with this oversight.

On MOON LANDING's first screen, you can see the machine language Display String subroutine and the ship's graphics as "garbage" at the bottom of the screen.  This is normal, and it's absolutely fine because you can't maneuver your lunar lander down toward the bottom of the screen.  After you land your craft successfully, your next task is to reach the "MotherCraft" on a second screen.  This second screen has NO boundary checking.    Just like in outer space, you can fly your lunar lander wherever you want to go.  On the second screen of MOON LANDING, if you fly all over the screen, then you may land in trouble.  In this case, you don't crash into the moon.  Rather, you crash (quite literally) the machine language routine.  Ouch, that's gotta hurt!

What's that?  You don't quite grasp what I'm talking about?  How can you fly your ship into a machine language subroutine?  What kind of nonsense is that?  Take a second to think this over.  If you can fly your lunar lander ANYWHERE on the screen (which, remember, is all screen RAM), then is it possible that this could cause a problem?  You know... a problem toward the bottom of the screen?  Yes, flying anywhere sure can cause issues!  That's right, you got it!  You can fly your lunar lander right into the area of RAM at the bottom of the screen that holds the ML routine that displays your ship.  The moment that you do that, the game crashes spectacularly-- and your dead.  I didn't even have to reset the system after the crash... as the game crashed so badly that after some terrible clutter appeared on the screen, then the game was back to the BASIC prompt and the program was wiped from memory.  So much for that four minutes dedicated to loading MOON LANDING from tape into BASIC!

This game-ending crash is really too bad, as otherwise MOON LANDING seems like a solid effort and a fun game that makes pretty-good use of BASIC's ability to use machine language subroutines.  Can anyone else think of any released games (for ANY system) that crash so easily, predictably and wonderfully as MOON LANDING?

Adam

While looking through the disassembly of COSMIC RAIDERS, I noticed that the initial menu (which allows you to select the cartridge or the built-in games) directly grabs the "SELECT GAME" string from the on-board ROM.  First, this is unusual, because nearly all of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade games don't call this first menu from the cartridge.  Most games allow the on-board ROM to select the game before control passes to the cartridge.  However, like TREASURE COVE, the COSMIC RAIDERS cartridge takes control right away.  One of the first things that COSMIC RAIDERS does is to call the MENU routine.

This bring us back to this direct access at the on-board ROM's memory.  Would this work on the earliest Home Library Computer ROM?  The HLC ROM is usually called the "3164 ROM" due to the "GAME OVER" string being at location 3164 ($0C5C) in the ROM.  I don't have the Home Library Computer (I think most of these were only sold by JS&A), but I do have MAME, so I started it with this older ROM with this command line:

mamed astrocdl -cart cosmicrd -debug

After testing COSMIC RAIDERS with the 3164 ROM, the menu doesn't display the correct string!  Instead of displaying "SELECT GAME" at the top of the menu, COSMIC RAIDERS only displays "ING" (the last letters from SCRIBBLING).  Take a look at the screenshots I've attached to see what I mean.

This is the first time I can remember a cartridge (and not a BASIC program) running differently between the various ROMs.  I did play the beginning of COSMIC RAIDERS on the 3164 ROM; it seems to play okay-- only that first menu seems to be effected.

Do any other cartridge games act differently on various Bally Arcade/Astrocade systems with different ROMS?

Adam

 When I got to work I had a thought, even though it doesn't make good sense why they would do it. In hardware, especially back in the day when you wanted to save money on additional chips, the ports were sometimes only partially decoded. This would mean that there would be multiple ports you might use in the upper ranges that would really just be decoded as if you used the "real" ports. Perhaps $CC decodes in hardware to one of the "real" ports. 

 Again, it doesn't make sense to me why this would be done but thought I would throw it out there as a brainstorming session idea.

I use on of two joysticks when I'm emulating the Astrocade under MAME:


1) Atari 2600 controller (CX40) with the original Stelladapter.  This adapter hasn't been sold since, I think, 2009, but you can read about the specs and build you own here:


http://www.grandideastudio.com/stelladaptor-2600/


There is also the 2600-dapter, which does pretty-much the same thing, but works with FAR more controllers.   I own this adapter too-- I just don't use it that often.  The 2600-dapter can be bought here:


http://www.2600-daptor.com/


2) Ideally, if you want a "true" Bally Arcade/Astrocade experience (or as close as you can get with MAME's emulation of the hardware), then you can use an Astrocade controller with the Astro-daptor:


http://www.2600-daptor.com/Astro-daptor.htm


The Astro-daptor works really well with both modes of the Astrocade hand controller: the knob (i.e. "paddle") and the eight-direction "joystick."  The Astro-dapter can be purchased here:


http://www.2600-daptor.com/Astro-daptor.htm

The Bally maps out all inputs through SENTRY. The only reason I can think of it not working is that you may have a bad cell in one of your memory chips. That would cause possible erratic behavior of the SENTRY latch. The RWB Utility will NOT check the 4000h region of memory. You may need to do a program that checks all bits (or bytes) of screen ram. DO NOT CHECK THE STACK AREA as it will crash the program and maybe mess up something you may have in expanded memory.I can write you a program in either BASIC or machine language that will do a thorough check of each bit under various conditions.Of course you could have a bad I/O, ROM, ADDRESS, or DATA chip causing this condition, also.
As far as GA not pausing, that could be that they mapped it out in their SENTRY setup.Ken
